NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning

Jianhao Zhang Affiliation: Hangzhou Institute for Advanced StudyUniversity of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou, China, Email: zhangjianhao24@mails.ucas.ac.cn    Ou Wu Affiliation: Hangzhou Institute for Advanced StudyUniversity of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou, China, Email: wuou@ucas.ac.cn    Yi Du Affiliation: Hangzhou Institute for Advanced StudyUniversity of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou, China, Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Email: duyi@cnic.cn
Abstract

Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility–diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility–diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility–diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.

11footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications [1, 2]. As practical demands evolve, these models are often fine-tuned on new target data to adapt to emerging tasks [3, 4, 5]. However, recent studies indicate that adapting to new data can also erode previously acquired capabilities [6, 7], even after a single fine-tuning stage, resulting in catastrophic forgetting [8, 9, 10, 11, 12].

Recent advances have explored diverse strategies for mitigating catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning. Rehearsal-based methods revisit historical samples to preserve prior capabilities [13, 14], while representation-based methods mitigate forgetting through representational constraints [15, 16]. However, these methods generally assume access to pretraining data, which is often unavailable in realistic deployment settings. This limitation has motivated alternative approaches that do not rely on prior data, such as model merging [17], selective parameter updates [18], and importance weighting [11]. Recently, work has begun to leverage synthetic data for forgetting mitigation [19, 20].

Synthetic data offers a promising avenue for mitigating forgetting, yet the resulting candidate pools are often noisy and highly redundant, making effective data selection crucial [20, 21]. Many existing methods typically rely on indirect proxy signals such as perplexity to estimate sample utility, but these signals are not always well aligned with the actual training benefit [22, 23, 24]. Consequently, selected samples may appear plausible while contributing limited practical value [25, 26, 27]. To alleviate redundancy, prior work often incorporates diversity-promoting strategies [28, 29]. However, such strategies are often decoupled from utility estimation, making it difficult to jointly optimize sample quality and diversity. While determinantal point processes (DPPs) [30] provide an effective approach, their direct optimization is often computationally expensive for large-scale candidate pools, requiring O⁡(K​N​d)O(KNd)~[31] or O⁡(K​N​(d+log⁡N))O(KN(d+\log N)) [32] to select KK samples from a pool of size NN. These limitations leave an unresolved challenge of how to perform training-aware and diversity-aware selection efficiently over large-scale synthetic candidate pools.

To tackle these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a novel fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model deliberately exposes recipe-induced drift in pretrained behavior. This drift is then converted into a forgetting-aware utility for selecting synthetic samples as preservation constraints. NADS further combines this utility with diversity-aware subset construction through a scalable optimization procedure with iterative cost O⁡(T​N​(E+log⁡K))O(TN(E+\log K)). Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraint set through knowledge distillation (KD), preserving general capabilities during task adaptation.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose NADS, a novel fine-tuning framework for LLMs that uses recipe-conditioned navigator drift to guide data selection for forgetting mitigation. NADS trains a navigator under the target recipe without preservation regularization to deliberately expose drift in pretrained capabilities and then uses this drift to estimate the forgetting-aware utility of candidate samples.

  • •

    We formulate constraint set construction as a utility–diversity selection problem, and propose an efficient optimization strategy that renders this otherwise costly DPP-based formulation practical at scale. The resulting method reduces utility–diversity selection cost while preserving sample quality and diversity. We further provide theoretical analysis that motivates the proposed framework.

  • •

    We conduct extensive experiments across two benchmarks and three model families spanning 3B–9B parameters. Results show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task adaptation and general capability preservation, while achieving this with lower utility–diversity selection cost.

2 Related Work

2.1 Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning

Fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm for adapting large language models to evolving tasks and feedback, yet it often remains difficult to acquire new capabilities without degrading existing ones [33, 34, 35]. To mitigate forgetting, various approaches have been proposed. Regularization-based methods augment the training objective with importance-weighted penalties [36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41]. Rehearsal-based methods preserve prior knowledge by interleaving stored or synthesized samples during subsequent training [42, 19, 20, 43, 44]. Architecture-based methods reduce interference by isolating task-specific capacity, from expandable or modular designs to parameter-efficient tuning that restricts updates to lightweight components [45, 46, 47, 48]. Sample-space methods instead modulate the effective training signal via example reweighting, offering a lightweight way to balance stability and plasticity [11, 49, 50, 51]. While some replay methods use post-fine-tuning model-behavior changes to identify forgotten samples [52], NADS uses an unconstrained navigator before final constrained training to estimate forgetting-aware utility, enabling proactive synthetic-constraint selection from large candidate pools.

2.2 Data Selection in LLM Fine-Tuning

Data selection aims to filter training data that meet desired quality requirements, improving efficiency while maintaining comparable or near-lossless performance. Existing methods often do so using indirect proxy signals (e.g., reliability, consistency, or difficulty scores) to estimate sample usefulness for target adaptation [53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58]. Another line of work uses optimization-related proxy signals (e.g., gradients or influence scores) [59, 60, 61]. Recently, cross-model discrepancies have been explored for data selection [62, 63, 64]. Additionally, many methods encourage coverage to prevent the selected subset from collapsing into near duplicates, either through diversity diagnostics or explicit quality-diversity trade-offs [65, 66, 67, 68], or through structured objectives that directly favor non-overlapping evidence [69, 70, 71]. Although these methods improve data selection for fine-tuning, their selection objectives are mostly designed to improve target-task performance or reduce fine-tuning cost, rather than to select preservation constraints against update-induced forgetting.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem Definition

Let 𝜽\bm{\bm{\theta}} denote the model parameters. We consider a single-stage fine-tuning setting with a new-task dataset 𝒟new={(xi,yi)}i=1M\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M}, where the original pretraining data is unavailable but an auxiliary synthetic dataset 𝒞={xj}j=1N\mathcal{C}=\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} is accessible. NADS first constructs a navigator model MnavM_{\text{nav}} from the pretrained model MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} to select a constraint set 𝒟constraint⊂𝒞\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}}\subset\mathcal{C}. It then trains MfinalM_{\text{final}} on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} with KD regularization on 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}}, improving new-task performance while preserving the capabilities of MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}}. The overall framework is illustrated in Fig. 1.

3.2 Navigator Model Construction

Existing studies [62, 72, 63, 64] have explored model-centric data selection that measures the learning value of data through model change before and after training, thereby linking sample evaluation to its actual benefit for task adaptation. However, they primarily use the model to facilitate new-task adaptation, without exploring its potential to reveal update-induced forgetting during fine-tuning. Further discussion of the distinctions between these methods and NADS in Appendix A.

Motivated by this observation, we construct a model to trace the unconstrained adaptation path under the target recipe. This model is fine-tuned from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} without extra regularization, and therefore follows the realized training trajectory while naturally accumulating forgetting-related drift. Because it reveals how pretrained behavior drifts along this path and provides the guidance signal for subsequent forgetting-aware utility estimation, we refer to it as the navigator model MnavM_{\text{nav}}.

Checkpoint Selection and Local Deviation of the Navigator. The navigator serves as a reference along the unconstrained training trajectory. We select its checkpoint by validation-based early stopping, for which the following proposition gives a standard guarantee.

Because MnavM_{\text{nav}} is trained without constraint data or anti-forgetting regularization, it follows the unconstrained adaptation path and exhibits a more aggressive drift away from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}}. The following proposition locally controls deviation from this reference under bounded updates.

Appendix B.3 gives a conditional local perturbation view of navigator-side forgetting-risk ordering.

Concretely, we obtain MnavM_{\text{nav}} by fine-tuning MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} with validation-based early stopping. When validation data are unavailable or unreliable (e.g., data scarcity or label noise), we can use validation-free overfitting detection methods, such as the evolution of weight-matrix spectra [73]. We further analyze the performance and stability of MnavM_{\text{nav}} through experiments in Section 4.3.

3.3 Constraint Set Construction via Data Selection

When constructing 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}}, we aim to select samples that expose forgetting-related predictive drift under the target fine-tuning recipe while avoiding redundant selections. Since utility-only scoring can favor highly similar samples and sacrifice coverage, we formulate subset selection on the synthetic dataset 𝒞\mathcal{C} as a kk-DPP [74] to jointly account for utility and diversity under a fixed budget KK.

Definition 1 (kk-DPP).

Let 𝒞={xi}i=1N\mathcal{C}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} indexed by 𝒴={1,…,N}\mathcal{Y}=\{1,\ldots,N\}, and let S⊆𝒴S\subseteq\mathcal{Y} denote a selected set. For a real symmetric positive semidefinite kernel 𝐋∈ℝN×N\mathbf{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, the kk-DPP is defined by

ℙ⁡(S,𝐋)∝det(𝐋S),|S|=K,\mathbb{P}(S;\mathbf{L})\propto\det(\mathbf{L}_{S}),\qquad|S|=K, (1)

where 𝐋S\mathbf{L}_{S} is the principal submatrix of 𝐋\mathbf{L} indexed by SS.

Following [30], we adopt the standard LL-ensemble decomposition: (𝐋)i​j=qi​Gi​j​qj(\mathbf{L})_{ij}=q_{i}\,G_{ij}\,q_{j}, where qi∈ℝ+q_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} is the quality score of sample xix_{i} and 𝐆⪰0\mathbf{G}\succeq 0 is a similarity kernel capturing pairwise diversity.

Forgetting Utility. MnavM_{\text{nav}} reflects update-induced deviation from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} during task adaptation. We therefore use the forward KL divergence from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} to MnavM_{\text{nav}} as a forgetting-aware utility signal. Larger divergence then indicates higher preservation priority for samples that deviate more from pretrained behavior. However, not all large divergences are equally informative, as some may reflect noise or intrinsic uncertainty rather than forgetting-relevant changes. To suppress such spurious utility, we further apply a confidence gate derived from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}}. The resulting utility is defined as

ui=1|xi|∑t=1|xi|[DKL(Ppretrain(⋅∣xi,<t)∥Pnav(⋅∣xi,<t))⋅exp(−γH(Ppretrain(⋅∣xi,<t)))],u_{i}=\frac{1}{|x_{i}|}\sum\nolimits_{t=1}^{|x_{i}|}\bigg[D_{\text{KL}}\!\Big(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{i,<t})\,\big\|\,P_{\text{nav}}(\cdot\mid x_{i,<t})\Big)\cdot\exp\!\Big(-\gamma\,H\!\big(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{i,<t})\big)\Big)\bigg], (2)

where xix_{i} denotes the full sequence, H⁡(p)H(p) denotes entropy, and γ\gamma controls the confidence gate. As empirically supported by Fig. 2, higher-utility samples exhibit higher forgetting risk. To incorporate this utility into the kk-DPP formulation, we define qi≜exp⁡(ui/(2​β))q_{i}\triangleq\exp\left(u_{i}/(2\beta)\right), where β\beta controls the scaling. This yields an additive objective in uiu_{i}, linking utility estimation to subset selection. Appendix B.4 provides a local utility–KD alignment rationale, and Appendix D.3 shows that higher-utility candidates form more effective preservation constraints under the same KD objective.

Diversity Kernel. DPPs capture diversity through the determinant of the similarity submatrix 𝐆S\mathbf{G}_{S}, thereby favoring subsets whose elements are mutually dissimilar under 𝐆\mathbf{G}. To operationalize this property, we construct 𝐆\mathbf{G} as an inner-product Gram kernel [75] with Gi​j≜𝐳i⊤​𝐳jG_{ij}\triangleq\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_{j} and 𝐳i∈ℝd\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where dd is the embedding dimension, and adopt the stabilized diversity term logdet(𝐈K+𝐆S)\log\det(\mathbf{I}_{K}+\mathbf{G}_{S}) [76], where 𝐆S\mathbf{G}_{S} is the principal submatrix indexed by SS. Let 𝐙S=[𝐳i]i∈S∈ℝd×K\mathbf{Z}_{S}=[\mathbf{z}_{i}]_{i\in S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} so that 𝐆S=𝐙S⊤​𝐙S\mathbf{G}_{S}=\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{S}. Since this involves a K×KK\times K determinant, we apply Sylvester’s determinant identity [77] to rewrite it as

det(𝐈K+𝐙S⊤​𝐙S)=det(𝐈d+𝐙S​𝐙S⊤)=det(𝐈d+∑i∈S𝐳i​𝐳i⊤).\det(\mathbf{I}_{K}+\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{S})=\det(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\mathbf{Z}_{S}\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top})=\det\!\Big(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum\nolimits_{i\in S}\mathbf{z}_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\Big). (3)

Theorem 1 gives a unified objective that jointly balances forgetting-related utility and subset diversity. The full derivation is provided in Appendix C.1.

While Theorem 1 yields a principled objective, directly applying it to large-scale subset selection remains computationally costly. Moreover, existing greedy solvers [31, 32] rely on repeated gain evaluation during subset expansion, which quickly becomes a major bottleneck at scale.

3.4 Efficient Data Selection Algorithm

We propose a scalable subset selection strategy, as summarized in Algorithm 1. Specifically, we recast Eq. (4) into a sparse-weight surrogate that retains its utility–diversity structure while making the optimization tractable. To further enhance optimization stability, we incorporate an ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization term with strength ν\nu. The resulting objective is

F⁡(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​ui+β​log​det(𝐈d+∑i=1Nwi​𝐳i​𝐳i⊤)−ν2​‖𝐰‖22,𝐰∗=arg​max𝐰⪰𝟎,‖𝐰‖0=K⁡F​(𝐰).\!F(\mathbf{w})\!\triangleq\!\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}u_{i}+\beta\log\det\!\bigg(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\mathbf{z}_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\bigg)-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2},\quad\!\!\mathbf{w}^{*}=\!\!\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0},\,\|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}=K}\!\!F(\mathbf{w}). (5)

Further analysis of the discrepancy between Eq. (4) and Eq. (5) is provided in Appendix C.2.

Random Projection and Whitening. We apply a Johnson–Lindenstrauss random projection [78] to improve efficiency while preserving feature geometry. Let 𝐳i∈ℝd\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the sample-level representation of xix_{i}, obtained by mean pooling last-layer hidden states over non-padding tokens. After centering, we map the features into an EE-dimensional space using 𝐑∈ℝd×E\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times E} with E≪dE\ll d:

𝐳~i=𝐑⊤​(𝐳i−𝝁),𝝁=1N​∑i=1N𝐳i.\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}=\mathbf{R}^{\top}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{i}-\bm{\mu}\right),\quad\bm{\mu}=\frac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{z}_{i}. (6)

To further reduce feature anisotropy and off-diagonal coupling, we apply whitening [29] by computing 𝚺=1N​∑i=1N𝐳~i​𝐳~i⊤\bm{\Sigma}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top} and updating 𝐳~i←(𝚺+ρ​𝐈E)−12​𝐳~i\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\leftarrow(\bm{\Sigma}+\rho\mathbf{I}_{E})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}, where ρ\rho is a regularization constant.

Diagonal Approximation. Optimizing the log-determinant term remains computationally demanding, as the covariance still couples different feature dimensions. To obtain a more tractable objective, we introduce a diagonal approximation. Specifically, let 𝐀⁡(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​𝐳~i​𝐳~i⊤\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top} and replace logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰))\log\det(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})) with ∑e=1Elog⁡(1+Ae​e​(𝐰))\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log(1+A_{ee}(\mathbf{w})). Under this approximation, the objective becomes

F~​(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​ui+β​∑e=1Elog⁡(1+∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e 2)−ν2​‖𝐰‖22,𝐰⪰𝟎,‖𝐰‖0=K,\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}u_{i}+\beta\sum\nolimits_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\bigg(1+\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{\,2}\bigg)-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2},\quad\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0},~\|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}=K, (7)

where z~i,e\tilde{z}_{i,e} denotes the ee-th coordinate of 𝐳~i\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}, with diagonal error analysis in Appendix C.3.

Iterative Optimization. We adopt Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT) [79] for scalable optimization under the nonnegativity and KK-sparsity constraints. Specifically, we perform gradient ascent on F~​(𝐰)\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}), followed by a nonnegative hard-thresholding step that yields the weights at iteration tt

𝐰(t)=𝒫K((𝐰(t−1)+η∇F~(𝐰(t−1)))+),\mathbf{w}^{(t)}=\mathcal{P}_{K}\!\Big(\big(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}+\eta\,\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})\big)_{+}\Big), (8)

where η\eta is the step size, (⋅)+(\cdot)_{+} denotes elementwise nonnegativity truncation, and 𝒫K\mathcal{P}_{K} keeps the top-KK entries and sets the rest to zero. After TT iterations, we set S∗=ΩK​(𝐰(T))S^{*}=\Omega_{K}(\mathbf{w}^{(T)}) and construct 𝒟constraint={xi∣i∈S∗}\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}}=\{x_{i}\mid i\in S^{*}\}, where ΩK\Omega_{K} returns the top-KK indices. Appendices C.4, C.5, and C.6 provide the derivations of ∇F~​(𝐰)\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}) and Eq. (8), together with analysis of the iterative procedure.

Time Complexity Analysis. The selection-stage complexity of NADS is O⁡(N​E​d+E3+T⁡(N​E+N​log⁡K))O(NEd+E^{3}+T(NE+N\log K)). Random projection and whitening incur a one-time preprocessing cost of O⁡(N​E​d+E3)O(NEd+E^{3}), where the O⁡(N​E2)O(NE^{2}) whitening cost is dominated by O⁡(N​E​d)O(NEd) since E≪dE\ll d. In each iteration, computing 1+∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e21+\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2} takes O⁡(N​E)O(NE) time, and projecting onto the feasible set by retaining the top-KK entries costs O⁡(N​log⁡K)O(N\log K). By contrast, Fast Greedy [31] evaluates gains over the full candidate pool when adding each element, resulting in O⁡(K​N​d)O(KNd) complexity. Lazy-Fast variants [32] alleviate redundant gain evaluation via lazy updates, yet their reported overall complexity still remains O⁡(K​N​(d+log⁡N))O(KN(d+\log N)). Overall, our optimization yields a markedly more efficient route to optimizing a scalable surrogate of Eq. (4) and remains well suited to large candidate pools.

3.5 Learning with Knowledge Distillation

We train MfinalM_{\text{final}} on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} and 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}} via KD, where 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} supports target-task adaptation and 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}} provides capability-preserving supervision from MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}}. The overall training objective is

ℒfinal=ℒTask+λ​ℒKD,\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{Task}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}, (9)

where λ\lambda controls the distillation strength. Here, ℒTask\mathcal{L}_{\text{Task}} is the negative log-likelihood on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}, encouraging MfinalM_{\text{final}} to fit the target task, while ℒKD\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} uses MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} as a teacher on 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}} and penalizes deviations of MfinalM_{\text{final}} from pretrained predictive behavior on the selected constraint samples.

4 Experiments

We evaluate NADS along four key dimensions: Q1: Does NADS better balance target-task adaptation and general capability preservation than SOTA baselines? Q2: Does MnavM_{\text{nav}} provide an effective reference under the target recipe? Q3: Can NADS select more effective and diverse data with lower selection-stage overhead than alternative selection methods? Q4: Do the key components of NADS each contribute meaningfully, and does the framework remain robust across hyperparameter settings?

4.1 Experiment Setup

Datasets & Evaluation Metrics. We conduct experiments on Magicoder [80] and MetaMathQA [81] to evaluate NADS, using Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered [82] as the large-scale synthetic data source. Following recent studies [9, 10, 11, 83, 84], we decouple evaluation into target performance and general capability, with benchmark roles adjusted across scenarios. For Magicoder, HumanEval (HE) [85] is the target benchmark, while MMLU [86], HellaSwag (HASW) [87], GSM8K [88], and OpenBookQA (OBQA) [89] assess general capability. For MetaMathQA, GSM8K is the target benchmark, while HumanEval is moved to the general-capability suite. We report general capability (mean of four benchmarks), target performance, and Overall (arithmetic mean of the two).

Baselines & Implementation Details. We compare NADS with three baseline groups: 1) standard fine-tuning, including Standard Fine-Tuning (FT) and LoRA [90]; 2) replay-based constraint selection, including Random selection, InsCL [91], LER [92], and Mix-cd [52]; and 3) target-data selection, including LESS [59], FisherSFT [93], and SPICE [94]. We evaluate all methods on LLaMA3.2-3B [95], Gemma3-4B [96], and Qwen3.5-9B [97]. For each target dataset, we hold out 1,0001{,}000 examples for validation and use the remaining target-training split for all methods. Target-data selection methods select 10% of this split, whereas replay-based methods and NADS use the entire split with 5%5\% of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as constraints. For NADS, we set γ=0.7\gamma=0.7, ν=3×10−3\nu=3\times 10^{-3}, β=1.0\beta=1.0, λ=5\lambda=5, T=50T=50, and E=256E=256. We report mean and standard deviation over three seeds. Details are in Appendix E.

4.2 Main Results (Q1)

Comparison Results. Table 1 reports the main Magicoder comparison with replay-based constraint-selection methods. On LLaMA3.2, NADS achieves 42.52% general-capability and 43.46% overall averages, compared with 41.43% and 42.01% for the strongest baseline, while remaining competitive on the target task. Similar trends on Gemma3 and Qwen3.5 indicate stable gains across model scales. Since target-task data selection can also mitigate forgetting [8, 83, 98], Table 2 reports LESS, FisherSFT, and SPICE as cross-paradigm references, which select from 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} rather than constructing synthetic constraints. This reference comparison is not a direct ranking, but indicates that NADS remains competitive under a different selection paradigm. MetaMathQA results are in Appendix F.1.

As shown in Table 1, existing replay-based baselines partly mitigate the adaptation–preservation trade-off, but limited gains reflect selection signals that do not target update-induced forgetting. In contrast, NADS constructs the constraint set from navigator-induced predictive drift, making selected samples more sensitive to forgetting-related changes under the target recipe. This targeted, less redundant constraint set supports target-task adaptation while maintaining stronger general capability.

Controlled comparison with a fixed KD objective. A potential concern is that the gains of NADS in Table 2 may come from the additional KD objective rather than the selected constraint set. Since NADS selects synthetic constraints rather than new-task samples, using LESS, FisherSFT, or SPICE-selected data would evaluate a combined method instead of NADS itself. We therefore fix the KD objective and vary only the constraint source. We apply the same KD objective to three baselines with either random or navigator-selected constraints. As shown in Fig. 4, random constraints do not reliably preserve general capability and can even hurt retention, whereas navigator-selected constraints consistently improve it across baselines. This suggests that the improvement is not merely due to KD or additional constraint samples, but to the effectiveness of the selected constraints. Details are given in Appendix F.2.

4.3 Analysis of the Navigator Model (Q2)

The navigator MnavM_{\text{nav}} is central to NADS, providing the signal for estimating update-induced forgetting risk. Thus, we examine whether MnavM_{\text{nav}} is useful and stable in practice from the following two aspects.

Unconstrained Drift Behavior. Table 3 shows the performance of MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} and MnavM_{\text{nav}} on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2. MnavM_{\text{nav}} achieves much stronger new-task performance, indicating that it has effectively adapted to the target data. Meanwhile, because it is trained without any anti-forgetting constraints, this gain is accompanied by noticeable degradation on prior capability.

Training Dynamics of the Navigator Model. Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b) depict the dynamics of new-task performance and general capability throughout MnavM_{\text{nav}} training on LLaMA3.2-3B. As training proceeds, MnavM_{\text{nav}} improves on the new task while progressively degrading on prior capability, reflecting increasing update-induced drift. To further examine how the navigator training stage affects constraint-set construction, Fig. 3(c) compares NADS using MnavM_{\text{nav}}-1, MnavM_{\text{nav}}-2, and MnavM_{\text{nav}}-3 from three training stages. MnavM_{\text{nav}}-1 is trained too early and remains too close to MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}}, resulting in a weak forgetting-risk signal and a less informative constraint set. MnavM_{\text{nav}}-3 is trained for too long, causing more aggressive drift that biases forgetting-risk estimation and weakens general capability preservation. In contrast, MnavM_{\text{nav}}-2 achieves the best trade-off between target-task performance and general capability preservation. Additional checkpoint comparisons across models and target datasets and sensitivity analyses under validation-set perturbations are provided in Appendix F.3 and Appendix F.4, respectively.

4.4 Effectiveness and Efficiency of Data Selection (Q3)

We further analyze the data selection strategy of NADS from three perspectives by examining whether it can select higher-quality data, maintain greater diversity, and reduce selection cost.

Quality of the Selected Data. We compare NADS with Random, PPL-based, and DPP-based selection on LLaMA3.2-3B under the same final KD objective and DconstraintD_{\text{constraint}} budget. Selected-data quality is measured by downstream performance after training on each selected set. As shown in Table 4, the alternatives incur larger general-capability drops, indicating that NADS identifies higher-quality data.

Diversity of the Selected Set. We further examine whether the proposed strategy selects more diverse data on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B. As shown in Fig. 5(a), NADS achieves strong average pairwise cosine distance and log-det diversity among the compared methods, suggesting that it selects less redundant constraint samples. Fig. 5(b) further visualizes the selected samples using t-SNE [99] in the representation space, where the data selected by NADS are distributed more broadly than those selected by utility-oriented competing methods. Additional qualitative and quantitative comparisons with more selection methods are provided in Appendix F.5.

Data-Selection Efficiency. Fig. 5(c) compares the runtime and peak GPU memory of different data-selection methods for selecting 10% of the data under the same candidate pool and budget. The reported cost covers the selection stage, including method-specific score or utility computation, related preprocessing, and subset optimization. NADS reduces selection-stage runtime relative to competing methods while maintaining comparable peak GPU memory, demonstrating efficient large-scale data selection. We further compare the overhead after replacing our optimizer with Fast Greedy (NADS-FG) [31] and Lazy-Fast Greedy (NADS-LFG) [32]. The time overhead analysis of MnavM_{\text{nav}} and the performance–cost analysis of the complete training pipeline are provided in Appendix F.6. Stage-wise and total computational costs across model sizes, including the cost savings from LoRA-based Navigator training, are reported in Appendix F.8.

4.5 Ablation Study and Sensitivity Analysis (Q4)

Ablation Study. We conduct ablation studies to assess the key components of NADS. We first ablate the KL-discrepancy factor in the original utility, leaving only the pretrained confidence gate for scoring candidate samples. We also remove the diversity-aware selection term and the confidence gate in utility estimation. As shown in Table 5, all modifications underperform the full NADS. The gate-only utility causes the largest degradation, indicating that pretrained confidence alone is

insufficient and that navigator-induced predictive discrepancy provides essential forgetting-aware information. Removing the diversity-aware term or the confidence gate also consistently hurts performance, validating the proposed utility and diversity design. We further compare utility signals in Fig. 6(a). Forward KL performs best, followed by JS divergence. This is consistent with the final KD objective, where the pretrained model serves as the teacher. Thus, measuring drift from the pretrained distribution provides a more aligned signal for selecting preservation constraints.

Hyperparameter Analysis. We conduct sensitivity analyses for the major hyperparameters in NADS. Fig. 6(b) shows that NADS remains effective over a broad range of settings. For most hyperparameters, moving from very small values to moderate ones improves performance, after which the curves largely plateau. The main exception is the distillation strength, which exhibits a clearer trade-off between target-task adaptation and general capability preservation. Larger values strengthen preservation, but overly strong distillation begins to hurt target-task performance. The best overall balance is therefore achieved in the intermediate regime.

Additional Robustness Analysis. We further examine whether NADS is sensitive to the candidate pool or constraint-set size. Results show that NADS remains effective across different candidate pools and constraint-set sizes, with detailed comparisons in Appendices F.9 and F.10. We also evaluate instruction-tuning performance using the Alpaca-GPT4 dataset [100] across ten general-capability benchmarks. Detailed experimental settings and results are provided in Appendix F.11.

4.6 Comparison with Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation Methods

We compare NADS with recent catastrophic-forgetting mitigation methods, including STM [8], NANOADAM [101], FLOW [11], DavIR [62], and TALR [10]. Fig. 6(c) reports the comparison on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B, where NADS achieves a favorable overall balance between new-task adaptation and general capability preservation. Detailed analyses and comparisons are in Appendix G.

5 Conclusion

We present NADS, a navigator-guided data selection framework for mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLM fine-tuning without pretraining data. By converting recipe-induced navigator drift into a forgetting-aware signal, NADS selects diverse synthetic constraints that support pretrained-behavior preservation. Experiments across tasks and model families show that NADS improves the adaptation–preservation trade-off with practical selection cost. These results indicate that navigator-induced predictive drift provides a useful bridge between target-task adaptation and preservation-constraint selection. Future work may explore lower-cost navigator construction and adaptive selection strategies.

Appendix A Comparison with Existing Model-Centric Data Selection Methods

In this section, we clarify the key distinction between the navigator model in NADS and the reference models adopted in prior model-centric data selection methods. Existing methods have shown that model differences can be used to construct informative selection signals. DavIR [62] scores samples by comparing the loss difference between the pretrained model and a reference model fine tuned on the full training set, and treats this score as an implicit reward. The resulting signal mainly reflects how much a sample contributes to target task adaptation. ToV [72] updates the model using a small validation set from the target distribution, and then scores samples according to the loss change before and after this update. Its reference model therefore also serves target domain utility estimation. TOSS [63] trains a safety-degraded model and a utility-oriented model on harmful reference data and high quality reference data, respectively, and identifies unsafe tokens through their loss difference. Forgetting [64] further fine tunes the base model on a sampled reference subset, and uses the resulting token level influence score to partition tokens for subsequent learning or forgetting. These methods use reference model differences for their respective selection or partitioning objectives.

The navigator in NADS is designed for a different role. It is obtained by applying the same target task adaptation recipe used in the final fine-tuning stage, but without retention regularization or constraint samples. The resulting navigator provides a recipe-conditioned estimate of forgetting risk for candidate constraint samples by comparing its predictions with those of the pretrained model. A larger predictive divergence indicates that the pretrained behavior on the sample is more likely to be altered under unconstrained target task adaptation. NADS therefore selects samples with higher estimated forgetting risk as preservation samples for the final fine-tuning stage.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis

B.1 Proof of Proposition 1

In this section, we prove that the checkpoint selected by validation-based early stopping is near-best on the unconstrained adaptation trajectory.

Proof. Let {𝜽t}t=0T\{\bm{\theta}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T} denote the unconstrained adaptation trajectory induced by the target recipe. Along this trajectory, define R⁡(t)≜ℒpop​(𝜽t)R(t)\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{\text{pop}}(\bm{\theta}_{t}) and R^​(t)≜ℒval​(𝜽t)\hat{R}(t)\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\bm{\theta}_{t}), where R⁡(t)R(t) is the population new-task risk at checkpoint 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t}, and R^​(t)\hat{R}(t) is the empirical validation loss on the held-out validation set. Let

topt∈arg​mint∈{0,…,T}⁡R​(t),t∗∈arg​mint∈{0,…,T}⁡R^​(t),t_{\text{opt}}\in\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{t\in\{0,\dots,T\}}R(t),\qquad t^{*}\in\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{t\in\{0,\dots,T\}}\hat{R}(t), (10)

where toptt_{\text{opt}} denotes the population-risk minimizer along the unconstrained adaptation trajectory, and t∗t^{*} denotes the checkpoint selected by validation-based early stopping. By the definition of t∗t^{*}, we have R^​(t∗)≤R^​(t)\hat{R}(t^{*})\leq\hat{R}(t) for all t∈{0,…,T}t\in\{0,\dots,T\}. In particular, taking t=toptt=t_{\text{opt}} gives

R^​(t∗)≤R^​(topt).\hat{R}(t^{*})\leq\hat{R}(t_{\text{opt}}). (11)

By assumption, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that |R^​(t)−R⁡(t)|≤ε|\hat{R}(t)-R(t)|\leq\varepsilon holds for all t∈{0,…,T}t\in\{0,\dots,T\}. Equivalently,

R⁡(t)−ε≤R^​(t)≤R⁡(t)+ε,∀t∈{0,…,T}.R(t)-\varepsilon\leq\hat{R}(t)\leq R(t)+\varepsilon,\qquad\forall t\in\{0,\dots,T\}. (12)

Applying the left inequality in Eq. (12) at t=t∗t=t^{*} and the right inequality at t=toptt=t_{\text{opt}}, and combining them with Eq. (11), we obtain

R⁡(t∗)−ε≤R^​(t∗)≤R^​(topt)≤R⁡(topt)+ε.R(t^{*})-\varepsilon\leq\hat{R}(t^{*})\leq\hat{R}(t_{\text{opt}})\leq R(t_{\text{opt}})+\varepsilon. (13)

Rearranging Eq. (13) yields R⁡(t∗)−R⁡(topt)≤2​εR(t^{*})-R(t_{\text{opt}})\leq 2\varepsilon. Therefore, the validation-selected checkpoint has population new-task risk within 2​ε2\varepsilon of the best checkpoint on the unconstrained adaptation trajectory.

B.2 Proof of Proposition 2

In this section, we prove the local deviation recursion in Proposition 2, showing that bounded preservation updates control the mismatch between the training trajectory of MfinalM_{\text{final}} and the unconstrained target-task trajectory over local horizons.

Proof. Let dt:=‖𝜽t−𝜽¯t‖d_{t}:=\|\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\| denote the deviation between the constrained trajectory {𝜽t}t=0T\{\bm{\theta}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T} and the unconstrained trajectory {𝜽¯t}t=0T\{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T} at step tt. By the update rules 𝜽t+1=𝜽t−η⁡(∇Ltask​(𝜽t)+ξt)\bm{\theta}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\eta\bigl(\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bm{\theta}_{t})+\xi_{t}\bigr) and 𝜽¯t+1=𝜽¯t−η∇Ltask(𝜽¯t)\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}=\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}-\eta\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}), their difference satisfies

𝜽t+1−𝜽¯t+1=𝜽t−𝜽¯t−η⁡(∇Ltask​(𝜽t)−∇Ltask​(𝜽¯t))−η​ξt.\bm{\theta}_{t+1}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+1}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}-\eta\bigl(\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bm{\theta}_{t})-\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t})\bigr)-\eta\xi_{t}. (14)

Taking norms and applying the triangle inequality yields

dt+1≤dt+η​‖∇Ltask​(𝜽t)−∇Ltask​(𝜽¯t)‖+η​‖ξt‖.d_{t+1}\leq d_{t}+\eta\|\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bm{\theta}_{t})-\nabla L_{\text{task}}(\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t})\|+\eta\|\xi_{t}\|. (15)

By the LL-Lipschitz continuity of ∇Ltask\nabla L_{\text{task}} and the bound ‖ξt‖≤κ\|\xi_{t}\|\leq\kappa, we obtain dt+1≤(1+η​L)​dt+η​κd_{t+1}\leq(1+\eta L)d_{t}+\eta\kappa. Then, we fix a reference step tt and an integer local horizon τ∈{0,…,T−t}\tau\in\{0,\dots,T-t\}. Iterating the one-step bound from step tt onward gives that, for any s∈{0,…,τ}s\in\{0,\dots,\tau\},

dt+s≤dt+∑j=0s−1η⁡(L​dt+j+κ).d_{t+s}\leq d_{t}+\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\eta\bigl(Ld_{t+j}+\kappa\bigr). (16)

Taking the supremum over 0≤s≤τ0\leq s\leq\tau on the left-hand side yields

sup0≤s≤τdt+s≤dt+∑j=0τ−1η⁡(L​dt+j+κ).\sup_{0\leq s\leq\tau}d_{t+s}\leq d_{t}+\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}\eta\bigl(Ld_{t+j}+\kappa\bigr). (17)

Substituting back dt=‖𝜽t−𝜽¯t‖d_{t}=\|\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\| proves

sup0≤s≤τ‖𝜽t+s−𝜽¯t+s‖≤‖𝜽t−𝜽¯t‖+∑j=0τ−1η⁡(L​‖𝜽t+j−𝜽¯t+j‖+κ).\sup_{0\leq s\leq\tau}\|\bm{\theta}_{t+s}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+s}\|\leq\|\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t}\|+\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}\eta\bigl(L\|\bm{\theta}_{t+j}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+j}\|+\kappa\bigr). (18)

Therefore, bounded preservation updates locally control trajectory mismatch.

B.3 Local perturbation of navigator-side forgetting-risk ordering

Corollary 1 (Local perturbation of navigator-side forgetting-risk ordering).

Let Δθ​(x)\Delta_{\theta}(x) denote the forgetting-risk score of sample xx. Fix a reference step tt and an integer local horizon τ∈{0,…,T−t}\tau\in\{0,\dots,T-t\}, and let 𝒩t,τ\mathcal{N}_{t,\tau} denote a neighborhood containing the navigator and final trajectories over this horizon. Assume that, for each sample xx, Δθ​(x)\Delta_{\theta}(x) is Lipschitz on 𝒩t,τ\mathcal{N}_{t,\tau} with local constant Gt,τ​(x)G_{t,\tau}(x). Define the local trajectory mismatch Bt,τ:=sup0≤s≤τ‖𝛉t+s−𝛉¯t+s‖B_{t,\tau}\;:=\;\sup_{0\leq s\leq\tau}\|\bm{\theta}_{t+s}-\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+s}\|. Then, for any two samples xax_{a} and xbx_{b},

|[Δ𝜽t+τ​(xa)−Δ𝜽t+τ​(xb)]−[Δ𝜽¯t+τ​(xa)−Δ𝜽¯t+τ​(xb)]|≤(Gt,τ​(xa)+Gt,τ​(xb))​Bt,τ.\Big|[\Delta_{\bm{\theta}_{t+\tau}}(x_{a})-\Delta_{\bm{\theta}_{t+\tau}}(x_{b})]-[\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{a})-\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{b})]\Big|\leq\bigl(G_{t,\tau}(x_{a})+G_{t,\tau}(x_{b})\bigr)B_{t,\tau}.

Consequently, if |Δ𝛉¯t+τ​(xa)−Δ𝛉¯t+τ​(xb)|>(Gt,τ​(xa)+Gt,τ​(xb))​Bt,τ\big|\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{a})-\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{b})\big|>\bigl(G_{t,\tau}(x_{a})+G_{t,\tau}(x_{b})\bigr)B_{t,\tau}, then the pairwise ordering between xax_{a} and xbx_{b} is preserved at step t+τt+\tau, i.e.,

sign⁡(Δ𝜽t+τ​(xa)−Δ𝜽t+τ​(xb))=sign⁡(Δ𝜽¯t+τ​(xa)−Δ𝜽¯t+τ​(xb)).\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\Delta_{\bm{\theta}_{t+\tau}}(x_{a})-\Delta_{\bm{\theta}_{t+\tau}}(x_{b})\big)=\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{a})-\Delta_{\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{t+\tau}}(x_{b})\big).

Thus, this corollary is a conditional local perturbation statement. When the relevant score sensitivities are moderate and the local trajectory mismatch remains limited, pairwise orderings with sufficiently large navigator-side margins are preserved under the constrained final trajectory. Appendix D.1 provides an empirical analysis of this ordering fidelity by varying the KD strength and measuring the agreement between navigator-induced candidate rankings and final-trajectory reference rankings.

B.4 Theoretical connection between the KL-based utility and the KD objective

In this section, we clarify a local relation between the KL-based utility in NADS and the subset-level KD discrepancy in final training. We analyze how the utility shares the same token-level discrepancy as the KD objective, with an entropy-based reweighting that yields a confidence-aware local alignment with the capability-preserving regularizer at the navigator checkpoint.

For a sample xx, define the distillation discrepancy under model parameter 𝜽\bm{\theta} as

fx(𝜽):=1|x|∑t=1|x|DKL(Ppretrain(⋅∣x<t)∥P𝜽(⋅∣x<t)).f_{x}(\bm{\theta}):=\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x|}D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\,\big\|\,P_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\right). (19)

For a subset S⊆𝒞S\subseteq\mathcal{C}, define the corresponding set-level discrepancy as

FS​(𝜽):=1|S|​∑x∈Sfx​(𝜽).F_{S}(\bm{\theta}):=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}f_{x}(\bm{\theta}). (20)

Evaluating Eq. (20) at the navigator checkpoint 𝜽nav\bm{\theta}_{\text{nav}} yields the average KD discrepancy between the pretrained model and the navigator model over subset SS. The utility used in NADS is defined as

u(x)=1|x|∑t=1|x|wt(x)DKL(Ppretrain(⋅∣x<t)∥Pnav(⋅∣x<t)),u(x)=\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x|}w_{t}(x)\,D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\,\big\|\,P_{\text{nav}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\right), (21)

where wt(x)=exp(−γH(Ppretrain(⋅∣x<t)))w_{t}(x)=\exp\bigl(-\gamma H(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t}))\bigr). We define the set-level averaged utility as

U¯​(S):=1|S|​∑x∈Su⁡(x),U⁡(S):=∑x∈Su⁡(x).\bar{U}(S):=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}u(x),\qquad U(S):=\sum_{x\in S}u(x). (22)

Let δt(x):=DKL(Ppretrain(⋅∣x<t)∥Pnav(⋅∣x<t))\delta_{t}(x):=D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(P_{\text{pretrain}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\,\big\|\,P_{\text{nav}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\right) denote the token-level KD discrepancy at the navigator checkpoint. Then both FS​(𝜽nav)F_{S}(\bm{\theta}_{\text{nav}}) and U¯​(S)\bar{U}(S) are constructed from the same set of token-level discrepancies {δt​(x)}\{\delta_{t}(x)\}:

FS​(𝜽nav)=1|S|​∑x∈S1|x|​∑t=1|x|δt​(x),U¯​(S)=1|S|​∑x∈S1|x|​∑t=1|x|wt​(x)​δt​(x).F_{S}(\bm{\theta}_{\text{nav}})=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x|}\delta_{t}(x),\qquad\bar{U}(S)=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x|}w_{t}(x)\,\delta_{t}(x). (23)

Hence, the utility and the KD discrepancy share the same underlying signal, differing only in whether token-level contributions are reweighted.

Importantly, the entropy gate wt​(x)=exp⁡(−γ​H​(⋅))w_{t}(x)=\exp(-\gamma H(\cdot)) is monotone decreasing in the pretrained entropy. Thus, high-entropy positions are systematically down-weighted, whereas low-entropy positions contribute more strongly to the utility. This yields a confidence-aware reweighting of the KD discrepancy rather than an arbitrary transformation of the signal. Under this view, U¯​(S)\bar{U}(S) can be interpreted as a confidence-aware, robustness-oriented proxy of FS​(θnav)F_{S}(\theta_{\text{nav}}): it preserves the same discrepancy structure while reducing the influence of positions more likely to reflect intrinsic uncertainty or token-level noise.

This provides a local alignment rationale for the utility design in NADS. The final training objective reduces the KD discrepancy on the selected constraint set, while the selection utility evaluates the same navigator-side discrepancy with confidence-aware reweighting. Hence, the selection signal remains locally aligned with the KD objective while being less sensitive to high-entropy discrepancy patterns. Since γ≥0\gamma\geq 0 and 0≤H⁡(⋅)≤log⁡|V|0\leq H(\cdot)\leq\log|V|, the gate satisfies |V|−γ≤wt​(x)≤1|V|^{-\gamma}\leq w_{t}(x)\leq 1, implying |V|−γ​FS​(𝜽nav)≤U¯​(S)≤FS​(𝜽nav)|V|^{-\gamma}F_{S}(\bm{\theta}_{\text{nav}})\leq\bar{U}(S)\leq F_{S}(\bm{\theta}_{\text{nav}}). This boundedness is mainly a consistency property; the primary role of the entropy gate is its monotone confidence-aware reweighting effect.

Overall, the KL-based utility and the KD regularizer are locally connected through the same navigator-side discrepancy. Around the navigator checkpoint, the utility serves as a confidence-aware proxy of this discrepancy, providing a locally aligned signal for constructing capability-preserving constraints. Appendix D.3 further examines this utility signal empirically by comparing constraint sets selected from different utility ranges under the same final KD objective.

Appendix C Derivation Details of the Selection Algorithm

C.1 Derivation of the Selection Objective

In this section, we derive the utility–diversity selection objective from the standard kk-DPP formulation. We start from

S∗=arg​maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K​log​det(𝐋S),S^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\,|S|=K}\log\det(\mathbf{L}_{S}), (24)

where 𝐋S\mathbf{L}_{S} denotes the principal submatrix of the LL-ensemble kernel indexed by the subset SS. Following the LL-ensemble decomposition, let 𝐋=𝐐𝐆𝐐\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Q}, where 𝐐≜diag​(q1,…,qN)\mathbf{Q}\triangleq\text{diag}(q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}) and 𝐆⪰0\mathbf{G}\succeq 0. For any subset SS, the corresponding principal submatrix can be written as 𝐋S=𝐐S​𝐆S​𝐐S\mathbf{L}_{S}=\mathbf{Q}_{S}\,\mathbf{G}_{S}\,\mathbf{Q}_{S}, so taking determinants gives det(𝐋S)=det(𝐐S)​det(𝐆S)​det(𝐐S)\det(\mathbf{L}_{S})=\det(\mathbf{Q}_{S})\,\det(\mathbf{G}_{S})\,\det(\mathbf{Q}_{S}). Since 𝐐S\mathbf{Q}_{S} is diagonal, det(𝐐S)=∏i∈Sqi\det(\mathbf{Q}_{S})=\prod_{i\in S}q_{i}, and therefore det(𝐋S)=(∏i∈Sqi2)​det(𝐆S)\det(\mathbf{L}_{S})=\Big(\prod_{i\in S}q_{i}^{2}\Big)\det(\mathbf{G}_{S}). Taking logarithms yields

logdet(𝐋S)=2∑i∈Slogqi+logdet(𝐆S).\log\det(\mathbf{L}_{S})=2\sum_{i\in S}\log q_{i}+\log\det(\mathbf{G}_{S}). (25)

Substituting Eq. (25) into Eq. (24) gives the equivalent objective

S∗=arg​maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K(2∑i∈Slogqi+logdet(𝐆S)).S^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\,|S|=K}\left(2\sum_{i\in S}\log q_{i}+\log\det(\mathbf{G}_{S})\right). (26)

We next substitute the quality parametrization qi≜exp⁡(ui/(2​β))q_{i}\triangleq\exp\!\big(u_{i}/(2\beta)\big) with β>0\beta>0. Under this choice, and noting that multiplying the objective by the positive constant β\beta does not change the argmax, Eq. (26) becomes

S∗=arg​maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K(1β∑i∈Sui+logdet(𝐆S))=arg​maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K(∑i∈Sui+βlogdet(𝐆S)),S^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\,|S|=K}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}+\log\det(\mathbf{G}_{S})\right)=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\,|S|=K}\left(\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}+\beta\,\log\det(\mathbf{G}_{S})\right), (27)

Finally, we instantiate 𝐆\mathbf{G} as a Gram kernel built from the sample embeddings 𝐳i∈ℝd\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, so that 𝐆S=𝐙S⊤​𝐙S\mathbf{G}_{S}=\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{S}, where 𝐙S≜[𝐳i]i∈S∈ℝd×K\mathbf{Z}_{S}\triangleq[\mathbf{z}_{i}]_{i\in S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K}. To improve numerical stability and avoid rank deficiency, we replace logdet(𝐆S)\log\det(\mathbf{G}_{S}) with the stabilized diversity term logdet(𝐈K+𝐆S)\log\det(\mathbf{I}_{K}+\mathbf{G}_{S}) [76] and apply Sylvester’s determinant identity [77]:

det(𝐈K+𝐙S⊤​𝐙S)=det(𝐈d+𝐙S​𝐙S⊤)=det(𝐈d+∑i∈S𝐳i​𝐳i⊤).\det(\mathbf{I}_{K}+\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top}\mathbf{Z}_{S})=\det(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\mathbf{Z}_{S}\mathbf{Z}_{S}^{\top})=\det\!\Big(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{i\in S}\mathbf{z}_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\Big). (28)

Using this stabilized diversity term, Sylvester’s identity gives the objective

S∗=arg​maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K∑i∈Sui+βlogdet(𝐈d+∑i∈S𝐳i𝐳i⊤),S^{*}=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\,|S|=K}\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}+\beta\log\det\!\left(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{i\in S}\mathbf{z}_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\right), (29)

which is the stabilized utility–diversity objective used in the main text.

C.2 Objective Discrepancy Between the Discrete and Sparse Objectives

In this section, we analyze the discrepancy between the discrete subset-selection objective in Eq. (4) and the sparse continuous objective in Eq. (5).

Let Fdisc​(S)F_{\text{disc}}(S) denote the discrete objective in Eq. (4), F0​(𝐰)F_{0}(\mathbf{w}) the unregularized sparse objective, and Fspr​(𝐰)≜F0​(𝐰)−ν2​‖𝐰‖22F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq F_{0}(\mathbf{w})-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2} the full sparse objective in Eq. (5). For any subset S⊆[N]S\subseteq[N] with |S|=K|S|=K, let 𝟏S∈{0,1}N\mathbf{1}_{S}\in\{0,1\}^{N} be its indicator vector. Then, by direct substitution, F0​(𝟏S)=Fdisc​(S)F_{0}(\mathbf{1}_{S})=F_{\text{disc}}(S). This shows that the unregularized sparse objective exactly recovers the discrete objective when the weights are restricted to binary indicator vectors. For each coordinate,

∂F0​(𝐰)∂wi=ui+β​𝐳i⊤​(𝐈d+∑j=1Nwj​𝐳j​𝐳j⊤)−1​𝐳i.\frac{\partial F_{0}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{i}}=u_{i}+\beta\,\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\Bigl(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\Bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{z}_{i}. (30)

Since 𝐈d+∑j=1Nwj​𝐳j​𝐳j⊤⪰𝐈d\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\succeq\mathbf{I}_{d}, we have (𝐈d+∑j=1Nwj​𝐳j​𝐳j⊤)−1⪯𝐈d\Bigl(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\Bigr)^{-1}\preceq\mathbf{I}_{d}. Hence

0≤𝐳i⊤​(𝐈d+∑j=1Nwj​𝐳j​𝐳j⊤)−1​𝐳i≤‖𝐳i‖22,0\leq\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\Bigl(\mathbf{I}_{d}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\top}\Bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{z}_{i}\leq\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}, (31)

which implies |∂F0​(𝐰)∂wi|≤|ui|+β​‖𝐳i‖22\left|\frac{\partial F_{0}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{i}}\right|\leq|u_{i}|+\beta\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. Let L≜max1≤i≤N⁡(|ui|+β​‖𝐳i‖22)L\triangleq\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(|u_{i}|+\beta\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr). Then ‖∇F0​(𝐰)‖∞≤L\|\nabla F_{0}(\mathbf{w})\|_{\infty}\leq L uniformly over the feasible region. Now fix any 𝐰⪰0\mathbf{w}\succeq 0 with ‖𝐰‖0=K\|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}=K, and let S={i:wi≠0}S=\{i:\,w_{i}\neq 0\} denote its induced support. Because both 𝐰\mathbf{w} and 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} are nonnegative and supported on SS, every point on the line segment ξ⁡(τ)=𝟏S+τ⁡(𝐰−𝟏S)\xi(\tau)=\mathbf{1}_{S}+\tau(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}) for τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1] remains nonnegative and supported on SS, and the matrix inside the log-determinant remains positive definite along this segment. Applying the mean-value theorem, there exists some τ¯∈(0,1)\bar{\tau}\in(0,1) such that F0​(𝐰)−F0​(𝟏S)=⟨∇F0​(ξ⁡(τ¯)),𝐰−𝟏S⟩F_{0}(\mathbf{w})-F_{0}(\mathbf{1}_{S})=\left\langle\nabla F_{0}(\xi(\bar{\tau})),\,\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}\right\rangle. Hence,

|F0​(𝐰)−Fdisc​(S)|\displaystyle|F_{0}(\mathbf{w})-F_{\text{disc}}(S)| =|F0​(𝐰)−F0​(𝟏S)|≤‖∇F0​(ξ⁡(τ¯))‖∞​‖𝐰−𝟏S‖1≤L​‖𝐰−𝟏S‖1.\displaystyle=|F_{0}(\mathbf{w})-F_{0}(\mathbf{1}_{S})|\leq\|\nabla F_{0}(\xi(\bar{\tau}))\|_{\infty}\,\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}\|_{1}\leq L\,\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}\|_{1}. (32)

Using the definition of FsprF_{\text{spr}}, we further have

Fspr​(𝐰)−Fdisc​(S)=F0​(𝐰)−Fdisc​(S)−ν2​‖𝐰‖22.F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w})-F_{\text{disc}}(S)=F_{0}(\mathbf{w})-F_{\text{disc}}(S)-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2}. (33)

Combining this with the previous bound yields

−L​‖𝐰−𝟏S‖1−ν2​‖𝐰‖22≤Fspr​(𝐰)−Fdisc​(S)≤L​‖𝐰−𝟏S‖1−ν2​‖𝐰‖22.-\,L\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2}\;\leq\;F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w})-F_{\text{disc}}(S)\;\leq\;L\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{1}_{S}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2}. (34)

Eq. (34) shows that the discrepancy between the sparse objective and its corresponding discrete subset objective is controlled by the deviation of the relaxed weights from the binary indicator vector and the explicit quadratic regularization term.

Let 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} be any global maximizer of Eq. (5), and let S∗={i:wi∗≠0}S^{*}=\{i:\,w_{i}^{*}\neq 0\} be the selected index set induced by 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*}. Applying Eq. (34) to 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} gives

−L​‖𝐰∗−𝟏S∗‖1−ν2​‖𝐰∗‖22≤Fspr​(𝐰∗)−Fdisc​(S∗)≤L​‖𝐰∗−𝟏S∗‖1−ν2​‖𝐰∗‖22.-\,L\|\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\;\leq\;F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w}^{*})-F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*})\;\leq\;L\|\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}. (35)

Finally, let Sdisc∗S^{*}_{\text{disc}} denote any optimizer of Eq. (4). By optimality of the discrete solution, Fdisc​(S∗)≤Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*})\leq F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}}). Combining this with the upper bound in Eq. (35), we obtain

Fspr​(𝐰∗)≤Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)+L​‖𝐰∗−𝟏S∗‖1−ν2​‖𝐰∗‖22.F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\leq F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}})+L\|\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}. (36)

On the other hand, since 𝟏Sdisc∗\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}_{\text{disc}}} is feasible for Eq. (5), optimality of 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} implies

Fspr​(𝐰∗)≥Fspr​(𝟏Sdisc∗)=Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)−ν2​‖𝟏Sdisc∗‖22=Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)−ν2​K.F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\geq F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}_{\text{disc}}})=F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}})-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}_{\text{disc}}}\|_{2}^{2}=F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}})-\frac{\nu}{2}K. (37)

Combining Eq. (36) and Eq. (37), we arrive at the sandwich bound

Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)−ν2​K≤Fspr​(𝐰∗)≤Fdisc​(Sdisc∗)+L​‖𝐰∗−𝟏S∗‖1−ν2​‖𝐰∗‖22.F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}})-\frac{\nu}{2}K\;\leq\;F_{\text{spr}}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\;\leq\;F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*}_{\text{disc}})+L\|\mathbf{w}^{*}-\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}}\|_{1}-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}. (38)

Therefore, Eq. (5) can be viewed as a subset-structured continuous relaxation of Eq. (4). On binary indicator vectors, the unregularized sparse objective exactly recovers the discrete objective, while the quadratic term acts as an explicit regularizer for the relaxed continuous weights. The optimal sparse objective value is bounded around the discrete optimum, with the gap controlled by the deviation from the binary indicator vector and the regularization term.

C.3 Error Bound for the Diagonal Log-Determinant Approximation

In this section, we show that the error induced by the diagonal log-determinant approximation is characterized by the spectrum of the normalized off-diagonal coupling matrix of the whitened covariance accumulator.

Let 𝐀⁡(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​𝐳~i​𝐳~i⊤∈ℝE×E\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E} with 𝐰⪰𝟎\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0}, and define 𝐁⁡(𝐰)≜𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}). Since each outer product 𝐳~i​𝐳~i⊤\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top} is positive semidefinite and each weight satisfies wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0, we have 𝐀⁡(𝐰)⪰𝟎\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\succeq\mathbf{0} and therefore 𝐁⁡(𝐰)≻𝟎\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w})\succ\mathbf{0}. Applying Hadamard’s inequality to 𝐁⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w}) gives det(𝐁⁡(𝐰))≤∏e=1E[𝐁⁡(𝐰)]e​e\det(\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w}))\leq\prod_{e=1}^{E}[\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}, with equality if and only if 𝐁⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w}) is diagonal. Taking logarithms yields

logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰))≤∑e=1Elog([𝐁(𝐰)]e​e).\log\det\!\big(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\big)\leq\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\big([\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}\big). (39)

Since [𝐁⁡(𝐰)]e​e=1+[𝐀⁡(𝐰)]e​e[\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}=1+[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}, we obtain

logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰))≤∑e=1Elog(1+[𝐀(𝐰)]e​e)=logdet(𝐈E+diag(𝐀(𝐰))).\log\det\!\big(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\big)\leq\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\big(1+[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}\big)=\log\det\!\big(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}))\big). (40)

Moreover, by the definition of 𝐀⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}), we have [𝐀⁡(𝐰)]e​e=∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e2[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}, and therefore

logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰))≤∑e=1Elog(1+∑i=1Nwiz~i,e2).\log\det\!\big(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\big)\leq\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}\right). (41)

Thus, the diagonal log-determinant term provides a valid Hadamard-based upper approximation to the original diversity term. We next characterize the induced approximation gap.

We decompose 𝐀⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}) into diagonal and off-diagonal components by defining 𝐃⁡(𝐰)≜𝐈E+diag⁡(𝐀⁡(𝐰))\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\mathbf{I}_{E}+\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})) and 𝐑⁡(𝐰)≜𝐀⁡(𝐰)−diag⁡(𝐀⁡(𝐰))\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})-\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})), so that 𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰)=𝐃⁡(𝐰)+𝐑⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})+\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{w}). Since 𝐀⁡(𝐰)⪰𝟎\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\succeq\mathbf{0}, the matrix 𝐃⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w}) is positive definite. We then define the normalized off-diagonal coupling matrix 𝐂⁡(𝐰)≜𝐃​(𝐰)−12​𝐑​(𝐰)​𝐃​(𝐰)−12\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{w})\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{-\frac{1}{2}}. Define the approximation gap

Δdiag(𝐰)≜logdet(𝐈E+diag(𝐀(𝐰)))−logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰)).\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\log\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}))\bigr)-\log\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\bigr). (42)

From the definition of 𝐂⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w}), we have 𝐑⁡(𝐰)=𝐃​(𝐰)12​𝐂​(𝐰)​𝐃​(𝐰)12\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{\frac{1}{2}}. It then follows that

𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰)=𝐃⁡(𝐰)+𝐑⁡(𝐰)=𝐃​(𝐰)12​(𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰))​𝐃​(𝐰)12.\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})+\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{\frac{1}{2}}. (43)

Taking determinants on both sides gives det(𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰))=det(𝐃⁡(𝐰))​det(𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰))\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)=\det\bigl(\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr). Taking logarithms and using 𝐃⁡(𝐰)=𝐈E+diag⁡(𝐀⁡(𝐰))\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{I}_{E}+\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})), we obtain

Δdiag(𝐰)=−logdet(𝐈E+𝐂(𝐰)).\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})=-\log\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr). (44)

The Hadamard inequality above immediately implies that Δdiag​(𝐰)≥0\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})\geq 0. Since

𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰)=𝐃​(𝐰)−12​(𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰))​𝐃​(𝐰)−12,\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w})^{-\frac{1}{2}}, (45)

and both 𝐃⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{w}) and 𝐈E+𝐀⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w}) are positive definite, 𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w}) is also positive definite. Let λ1,…,λE\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{E} be the eigenvalues of 𝐂⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w}). Then λj>−1\lambda_{j}>-1 for all jj, so log⁡(1+λj)\log(1+\lambda_{j}) is well defined. Since 𝐂⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w}) has zero diagonal, ∑j=1Eλj=Tr⁡(𝐂⁡(𝐰))=0\sum_{j=1}^{E}\lambda_{j}=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)=0. Therefore,

Δdiag(𝐰)=−logdet(𝐈E+𝐂(𝐰))=∑j=1E(λj−log(1+λj)),\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})=-\log\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)=\sum_{j=1}^{E}\left(\lambda_{j}-\log(1+\lambda_{j})\right), (46)

where the last equality uses ∑jλj=0\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}=0. This identity shows that the diagonal approximation gap is exactly determined by the spectrum of the normalized off-diagonal coupling matrix.

We next derive a split-spectrum upper bound. Let f⁡(x)=x−log⁡(1+x)f(x)=x-\log(1+x) on (−1,∞)(-1,\infty). For λj≥0\lambda_{j}\geq 0, Taylor’s theorem around zero gives f⁡(λj)=12​f′′​(ξj)​λj2f(\lambda_{j})=\frac{1}{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{j})\lambda_{j}^{2} for some ξj∈[0,λj]\xi_{j}\in[0,\lambda_{j}]. Since f′′​(x)=1/(1+x)2≤1f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/(1+x)^{2}\leq 1 for x≥0x\geq 0, we have f⁡(λj)≤λj2/2f(\lambda_{j})\leq\lambda_{j}^{2}/2. For λj<0\lambda_{j}<0, Taylor’s theorem gives f⁡(λj)=12​f′′​(ξj)​λj2f(\lambda_{j})=\frac{1}{2}f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{j})\lambda_{j}^{2} for some ξj∈[λj,0]\xi_{j}\in[\lambda_{j},0]. Since f′′​(x)=1/(1+x)2f^{\prime\prime}(x)=1/(1+x)^{2} is decreasing on (−1,∞)(-1,\infty), it is maximized over [λj,0][\lambda_{j},0] at x=λjx=\lambda_{j}. Hence f′′​(ξj)≤1/(1+λj)2f^{\prime\prime}(\xi_{j})\leq 1/(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}, and

λj−log⁡(1+λj)≤{12​λj2,λj≥0,λj22​(1+λj)2,λj<0.\lambda_{j}-\log(1+\lambda_{j})\leq\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{j}^{2},&\lambda_{j}\geq 0,\\[5.69054pt] \frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{2(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}},&\lambda_{j}<0.\end{cases} (47)

Applying this bound to all eigenvalues yields

0≤Δdiag​(𝐰)≤12​∑λj≥0λj2+12​∑λj<0λj2(1+λj)2.0\leq\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}\geq 0}\lambda_{j}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}<0}\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}}. (48)

The asymmetry between the two branches follows from the monotone decrease of f′′f^{\prime\prime}: positive eigenvalues admit a uniform quadratic bound, while negative eigenvalues approaching −1-1 introduce the amplification factor 1/(1+λj)21/(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}. Thus, the split-spectrum bound separates benign positive eigen-directions from negative eigen-directions that can amplify the log-determinant gap.

For comparison, define δ⁡(𝐰)≜λmin​(𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰))>0\delta(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\lambda_{\min}\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\bigr)>0. Since 1+λj≥δ⁡(𝐰)1+\lambda_{j}\geq\delta(\mathbf{w}) for all jj, the split-spectrum bound further implies the coarser conditioning-aware bound

0≤Δdiag​(𝐰)≤‖𝐂⁡(𝐰)‖F22​δ​(𝐰)2.0\leq\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\|_{F}^{2}}{2\delta(\mathbf{w})^{2}}. (49)

This coarser form highlights the role of conditioning but can be conservative when only a small part of the spectrum lies near −1-1.

For the relative gap used in the empirical diagnostics, let Dfull(𝐰)=logdet(𝐈E+𝐀(𝐰))D_{\text{full}}(\mathbf{w})=\log\det\bigl(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})\bigr). Following Appendix D.4, let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be a small numerical stabilizer. Then,

RelGapdiag​(𝐰)=Δdiag​(𝐰)|Dfull​(𝐰)|+ϵ≤12​∑λj≥0λj2+12​∑λj<0λj2(1+λj)2|Dfull​(𝐰)|+ϵ.\text{RelGap}_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})=\frac{\Delta_{\text{diag}}(\mathbf{w})}{|D_{\text{full}}(\mathbf{w})|+\epsilon}\leq\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}\geq 0}\lambda_{j}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}<0}\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}}}{|D_{\text{full}}(\mathbf{w})|+\epsilon}. (50)

This normalized form matches the relative approximation gap reported in Appendix D.4.

Finally, since ‖𝐂⁡(𝐰)‖F2=∑j=1Eλj2\|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{j=1}^{E}\lambda_{j}^{2}, the normalized off-diagonal energy can also be written entry-wise as

‖𝐂⁡(𝐰)‖F2=∑e≠f[𝐀⁡(𝐰)]e​f2(1+[𝐀⁡(𝐰)]e​e)​(1+[𝐀⁡(𝐰)]f​f).\|\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{e\neq f}\frac{[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ef}^{2}}{\bigl(1+[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ee}\bigr)\bigl(1+[\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{w})]_{ff}\bigr)}. (51)

Therefore, the approximation gap is small when the normalized off-diagonal energy is small and the negative spectrum of 𝐂⁡(𝐰)\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w}) stays away from −1-1, equivalently when δ⁡(𝐰)=λmin​(𝐈E+𝐂⁡(𝐰))\delta(\mathbf{w})=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{I}_{E}+\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{w})) is bounded away from zero. Thus, whitening can reduce the empirical diagonal approximation gap by lowering normalized off-diagonal coupling and improving the normalized covariance spectrum. Appendix D.4 evaluates the observed approximation gap and ranking consistency of the diagonal surrogate, while Appendix D.5 analyzes this bound on the final selected support by comparing the observed gap with the split-spectrum certificate.

C.4 Closed-Form Gradient for IHT

In this section, we derive the closed-form gradient ∇F~​(𝐰)\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}) used in the IHT update in Eq. (8). The surrogate objective in Eq. (7) is

F~​(𝐰)=∑i=1Nwi​ui+β​∑e=1Elog⁡(1+∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e2)−ν2​‖𝐰‖22.\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}u_{i}+\beta\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}\right)-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2}. (52)

For notational convenience, define the aggregated per-dimension energy as ae​(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e2a_{e}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\,\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2} for e=1,…,Ee=1,\ldots,E. Then the diversity term can be written as ∑e=1Elog⁡(1+ae​(𝐰))\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log(1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w})).

We differentiate the three terms in F~​(𝐰)\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}) separately. The linear utility term is immediate: since ∑j=1Nwj​uj\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}u_{j} is linear in 𝐰\mathbf{w}, its partial derivative with respect to wiw_{i} is ∂∂wi​∑j=1Nwj​uj=ui\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}u_{j}=u_{i}. For the diversity term, applying the chain rule gives

∂∂wi​∑e=1Elog⁡(1+ae​(𝐰))=∑e=1E11+ae​(𝐰)⋅∂ae​(𝐰)∂wi.\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{i}}\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\left(1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w})\right)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\frac{1}{1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w})}\cdot\frac{\partial a_{e}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{i}}. (53)

By the definition of ae​(𝐰)a_{e}(\mathbf{w}), we have ∂ae​(𝐰)∂wi=z~i,e2\frac{\partial a_{e}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{i}}=\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}. Substituting this into Eq. (53) yields

∂∂wi​∑e=1Elog⁡(1+ae​(𝐰))=∑e=1Ez~i,e21+ae​(𝐰).\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{i}}\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\!\left(1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w})\right)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\frac{\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}}{1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w})}. (54)

For the quadratic regularization term, we directly obtain ∂∂wi​(−ν2​‖𝐰‖22)=−ν​wi\frac{\partial}{\partial w_{i}}\left(-\frac{\nu}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_{2}^{2}\right)=-\nu w_{i}. Combining the derivatives of the linear utility term, the diversity term in Eq. (54), and the quadratic regularizer, the partial derivative of F~​(𝐰)\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}) with respect to wiw_{i} is

∂F~​(𝐰)∂wi=ui+β∑e=1Ez~i,e21+∑ℓ=1Nwℓ​z~ℓ,e2−νwi,i=1,…,N.\frac{\partial\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{i}}=u_{i}+\beta\sum_{e=1}^{E}\frac{\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}}{1+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}w_{\ell}\,\tilde{z}_{\ell,e}^{2}}-\nu w_{i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N. (55)

Accordingly, the full gradient vector is

∇F~​(𝐰)=[∂F~​(𝐰)∂w1,…,∂F~​(𝐰)∂wN]⊤.\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})=\left[\frac{\partial\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{1}},\ldots,\frac{\partial\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_{N}}\right]^{\top}. (56)

C.5 Closed-Form Projected Gradient Update

In this section, we derive the closed-form projected gradient update used in IHT. We consider the objective F~​(𝐰)\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}) defined in Eq. (7) and the constrained maximization problem

max𝐰∈𝒞F~(𝐰),𝒞≜{𝐰∈ℝN:𝐰⪰𝟎,∥𝐰∥0=K}.\max_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{C}}\ \tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}),\qquad\mathcal{C}\triangleq\big\{\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:\ \mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0},\ \|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}=K\big\}. (57)

We focus on the nondegenerate projection case where the thresholded vector has at least KK strictly positive entries after nonnegative truncation, as used in the closed-form derivation below. Starting from the current iterate 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}, we consider the first-order expansion of F~\tilde{F} around 𝐰(t−1)\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)},

F~(𝐰)≈F~(𝐰(t−1))+∇F~(𝐰(t−1))⊤(𝐰−𝐰(t−1)).\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})\approx\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})+\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})^{\top}(\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}). (58)

This local approximation shows that the ascent direction is given by the gradient ∇F~​(𝐰(t−1))\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}). Therefore, taking a first-order ascent step with step size η>0\eta>0 yields the intermediate iterate

𝐯(t)≜𝐰(t−1)+η∇F~(𝐰(t−1)).\mathbf{v}^{(t)}\triangleq\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}+\eta\,\nabla\tilde{F}\!\left(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}\right). (59)

Because the intermediate iterate may violate the nonnegativity and sparsity constraints, we project it back onto 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the Euclidean sense and define the next iterate as

𝐰(t)≜Π𝒞​(𝐯(t)),Π𝒞​(𝐯)≜arg​min𝐰∈𝒞⁡‖𝐰−𝐯‖22.\mathbf{w}^{(t)}\triangleq\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}\!\big(\mathbf{v}^{(t)}\big),\qquad\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{v})\triangleq\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{C}}\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}. (60)

Consider the projection subproblem min𝐰⪰𝟎,‖𝐰‖0=K⁡‖𝐰−𝐯‖22\min_{\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0},\,\|\mathbf{w}\|_{0}=K}\ \|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}\|_{2}^{2}. Under this condition, the projection onto the exact-KK nonnegative set is obtained by retaining KK positive coordinates. We first note that negative coordinates of 𝐯\mathbf{v} can never receive positive mass in the optimum. Indeed, for any coordinate ii with vi<0v_{i}<0 and any feasible wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0, we have (wi−vi)2≥(0−vi)2(w_{i}-v_{i})^{2}\geq(0-v_{i})^{2}. Hence replacing wiw_{i} by zero cannot increase the objective, so an optimal solution must satisfy wi=0w_{i}=0 whenever vi<0v_{i}<0. This reduces the problem to the nonnegative truncation 𝐯+≜(𝐯)+\mathbf{v}_{+}\triangleq(\mathbf{v})_{+}, where [𝐯+]i≜max⁡(vi,0)[\mathbf{v}_{+}]_{i}\triangleq\max(v_{i},0).

For any fixed index set S⊆{1,…,N}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} with |S|=K|S|=K, consider minimizing ‖𝐰−𝐯+‖22\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}_{+}\|_{2}^{2} over all nonnegative vectors 𝐰\mathbf{w} satisfying wi=0w_{i}=0 for all i∉Si\notin S. Once the support is fixed to SS, the objective is minimized by matching 𝐯+\mathbf{v}_{+} on the active coordinates, that is, by setting wi=v+,iw_{i}=v_{+,i} for i∈Si\in S and wi=0w_{i}=0 otherwise. Substituting this minimizer gives ‖𝐰−𝐯+‖22=∑i∉Sv+,i2\|\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{v}_{+}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i\notin S}v_{+,i}^{2}. Therefore, minimizing the projection objective is equivalent to choosing a set SS of size KK that maximizes the retained energy ∑i∈Sv+,i2\sum_{i\in S}v_{+,i}^{2}. The optimal set is thus given by the indices of the KK largest entries of 𝐯+\mathbf{v}_{+}. Let ΩK​(𝐯+)\Omega_{K}(\mathbf{v}_{+}) denote an index set corresponding to the KK largest entries of 𝐯+\mathbf{v}_{+}. Then the hard-thresholding operator applied after nonnegative truncation can be written componentwise as

[𝒫K​(𝐯+)]i={v+,i,i∈ΩK​(𝐯+),0,otherwise.[\mathcal{P}_{K}(\mathbf{v}_{+})]_{i}=\begin{cases}v_{+,i},&i\in\Omega_{K}(\mathbf{v}_{+}),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (61)

Therefore, under the same condition, the Euclidean projection onto 𝒞\mathcal{C} admits the closed form Π𝒞​(𝐯)=𝒫K​(𝐯+)\Pi_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{v})=\mathcal{P}_{K}\!\big(\mathbf{v}_{+}\big). Substituting this into Eq. (60), we obtain the IHT update

𝐰(t)=𝒫K((𝐰(t−1)+η∇F~(𝐰(t−1)))+).\mathbf{w}^{(t)}=\mathcal{P}_{K}\!\Big(\big(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}+\eta\,\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})\big)_{+}\Big). (62)

C.6 Convergence Analysis of IHT after Selection Stabilization

In this section, we establish the convergence behavior of the IHT iteration after the selected subset stabilizes. We consider the update

𝐰(t)=𝒫K((𝐰(t−1)+η∇F~(𝐰(t−1)))+),\mathbf{w}^{(t)}=\mathcal{P}_{K}\!\Big(\big(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}+\eta\,\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})\big)_{+}\Big), (63)

From Appendix C.4, the Hessian of F~\tilde{F} is

∇2F~(𝐰)=−β∑e=1E𝐬e​𝐬e⊤(1+ae​(𝐰))2−νI,𝐬e=(z~1,e2,…,z~N,e2)⊤,\nabla^{2}\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})=-\beta\sum\nolimits_{e=1}^{E}\frac{\mathbf{s}_{e}\mathbf{s}_{e}^{\top}}{(1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w}))^{2}}-\nu I,\qquad\mathbf{s}_{e}=\bigl(\tilde{z}_{1,e}^{2},\ldots,\tilde{z}_{N,e}^{2}\bigr)^{\top}, (64)

where ae​(𝐰)≜∑i=1Nwi​z~i,e2a_{e}(\mathbf{w})\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\tilde{z}_{i,e}^{2}. Assuming ν>0\nu>0, since β>0\beta>0 and each 𝐬e​𝐬e⊤\mathbf{s}_{e}\mathbf{s}_{e}^{\top} is positive semidefinite, we have ∇2F~​(𝐰)⪯−ν​I\nabla^{2}\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})\preceq-\nu I, so F~\tilde{F} is ν\nu-strongly concave. Moreover, since 𝐰⪰𝟎\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0} implies ae​(𝐰)≥0a_{e}(\mathbf{w})\geq 0, we have (1+ae​(𝐰))−2≤1(1+a_{e}(\mathbf{w}))^{-2}\leq 1. Because the projected-whitened features are fixed, there exists

L≜ν+β​∑e=1E‖𝐬e‖22<∞L\triangleq\nu+\beta\sum\nolimits_{e=1}^{E}\|\mathbf{s}_{e}\|_{2}^{2}<\infty (65)

such that ‖∇2F~​(𝐰)‖2≤L\|\nabla^{2}\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w})\|_{2}\leq L, hence ∇F~\nabla\tilde{F} is LL-Lipschitz. Let 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} be an accumulation point of the IHT sequence {𝐰(t)}\{\mathbf{w}^{(t)}\}, and define the truncated forward vector 𝐯¯∗≜(𝐰∗+η∇F~(𝐰∗))+\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}\triangleq\bigl(\mathbf{w}^{*}+\eta\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{*})\bigr)_{+}. Suppose that 𝐯¯∗\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*} satisfies the strict top-KK margin condition [𝐯¯∗](K)>[𝐯¯∗](K+1)[\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}]_{(K)}>[\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}]_{(K+1)}, where [𝐯¯∗](k)[\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}]_{(k)} is its kk-th largest entry. Since 𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{*} is an accumulation point, there exists a subsequence {𝐰(tk)}\{\mathbf{w}^{(t_{k})}\} with 𝐰(tk)→𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{(t_{k})}\to\mathbf{w}^{*}.

Define 𝐯¯(t)≜(𝐰(t)+η∇F~(𝐰(t)))+\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{(t)}\triangleq\bigl(\mathbf{w}^{(t)}+\eta\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)})\bigr)_{+}. Since ∇F~\nabla\tilde{F} is continuous, any convergent subsequence 𝐰(tk)→𝐰∗\mathbf{w}^{(t_{k})}\to\mathbf{w}^{*} induces the corresponding convergence 𝐯¯(tk)→𝐯¯∗\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{(t_{k})}\to\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}. Let

S∗≜ΩK​(𝐯¯∗),δ≜[𝐯¯∗](K)−[𝐯¯∗](K+1)>0.S^{*}\triangleq\Omega_{K}(\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}),\qquad\delta\triangleq[\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}]_{(K)}-[\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}]_{(K+1)}>0. (66)

Then there exists an index k0k_{0} such that ‖𝐯¯(tk)−𝐯¯∗‖∞<δ3\|\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{(t_{k})}-\bar{\mathbf{v}}^{*}\|_{\infty}<\frac{\delta}{3} for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}. For any i∈S∗i\in S^{*} and any j∉S∗j\notin S^{*}, the definition of δ\delta gives v¯i∗−v¯j∗≥δ\bar{v}_{i}^{*}-\bar{v}_{j}^{*}\geq\delta. Combining this with the above bound, we have v¯i(tk)≥v¯i∗−δ3\bar{v}_{i}^{(t_{k})}\geq\bar{v}_{i}^{*}-\frac{\delta}{3} and v¯j(tk)≤v¯j∗+δ3\bar{v}_{j}^{(t_{k})}\leq\bar{v}_{j}^{*}+\frac{\delta}{3} for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}, and therefore

v¯i(tk)−v¯j(tk)≥(v¯i∗−v¯j∗)−2​δ3≥δ3>0.\bar{v}_{i}^{(t_{k})}-\bar{v}_{j}^{(t_{k})}\geq(\bar{v}_{i}^{*}-\bar{v}_{j}^{*})-\frac{2\delta}{3}\geq\frac{\delta}{3}>0. (67)
