If the selected subset is fixed to S∗S^{*} from some iteration onward, for instance because the subsequent iterates remain in this stability neighborhood, the IHT dynamics reduce to projected gradient ascent over 𝒞S∗≜{𝐰⪰𝟎:wi=0​ for ​i∉S∗}\mathcal{C}_{S^{*}}\triangleq\{\mathbf{w}\succeq\mathbf{0}:\ w_{i}=0\text{ for }i\notin S^{*}\}, and the update takes the form

𝐰(t)=Π𝒞S∗(𝐰(t−1)+η∇F~(𝐰(t−1))).\mathbf{w}^{(t)}=\Pi_{\mathcal{C}_{S^{*}}}\Bigl(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)}+\eta\nabla\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}^{(t-1)})\Bigr). (68)

Since 𝒞S∗\mathcal{C}_{S^{*}} is convex and F~\tilde{F} is LL-smooth and ν\nu-strongly concave on it, standard projected-gradient ascent results imply that, for any 0<η≤1/L0<\eta\leq 1/L, the fixed-subset iteration converges to the unique maximizer 𝐰^S∗=arg​max𝐰∈𝒞S∗⁡F~​(𝐰)\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{S^{*}}=\operatornamewithlimits{arg\,max}_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{C}_{S^{*}}}\tilde{F}(\mathbf{w}). Thus, the strict margin condition ensures local support stability, and once the support is fixed, the dynamics converge to the unique subset-restricted optimum of the regularized diagonal surrogate.

C.7 Theoretical Analysis of the Selection Objective

This section provides a unified analysis of the gap between the original discrete objective in Eq. (4) and the final surrogate objective optimized in Eq. (7). We first decompose the end-to-end discrepancy into three explicit sources of error. We then further show that this discrepancy analysis implies near-optimality of the surrogate-induced subset under the original discrete objective.

C.7.1 Analysis of the Objective Value Under Eq. 4 and Eq. 7

Let Fdisc​(S)F_{\text{disc}}(S), Fspr​(w)F_{\text{spr}}(w), and F~​(w)\tilde{F}(w) denote the objectives in Eq. (4), Eq. (5), and Eq. (7), respectively. We further define Fpw​(w)F_{\text{pw}}(w) as the counterpart of Eq. (5) obtained by replacing the original features with the projected-and-whitened features 𝐳~i\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}. For a feasible sparse weight vector w⪰0w\succeq 0 with ‖w‖0=K\|w\|_{0}=K, let S⁡(w):={i:wi≠0}S(w):=\{i:w_{i}\neq 0\} denote the subset induced by ww. Then, by the triangle inequality, the discrepancy between Eq. (4) and Eq. (7) is bounded as

|Fdisc​(S⁡(w))−F~​(w)|≤|Fdisc​(S⁡(w))−Fspr​(w)|+|Fspr​(w)−Fpw​(w)|+|Fpw​(w)−F~​(w)|.\bigl|F_{\text{disc}}(S(w))-\tilde{F}(w)\bigr|\leq\bigl|F_{\text{disc}}(S(w))-F_{\text{spr}}(w)\bigr|+\bigl|F_{\text{spr}}(w)-F_{\text{pw}}(w)\bigr|+\bigl|F_{\text{pw}}(w)-\tilde{F}(w)\bigr|. (69)

The first term captures the discrepancy introduced by relaxing subset selection into continuous sparse optimization, together with the explicit ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization term. By Appendix C.2, this term satisfies

|Fdisc​(S⁡(w))−Fspr​(w)|≤L​‖w−𝟏S⁡(w)‖1+ν2​‖w‖22,\bigl|F_{\text{disc}}(S(w))-F_{\text{spr}}(w)\bigr|\leq L\|w-\mathbf{1}_{S(w)}\|_{1}+\frac{\nu}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}, (70)

where L:=max1≤i≤N⁡(|ui|+β​‖𝐳i‖22)L:=\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\bigl(|u_{i}|+\beta\|\mathbf{z}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr). The second term quantifies the distortion introduced by random projection and whitening. Since the utility and regularization terms cancel, we have

|Fspr(w)−Fpw(w)|=β|logdet(Id+∑i∈S⁡(w)wi𝐳i𝐳i⊤)−logdet(IE+∑i∈S⁡(w)wi𝐳~i𝐳~i⊤)|.\bigl|F_{\text{spr}}(w)-F_{\text{pw}}(w)\bigr|=\beta\Bigl|\log\det\Bigl(I_{d}+\sum_{i\in S(w)}w_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\top}\Bigr)-\log\det\Bigl(I_{E}+\sum_{i\in S(w)}w_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_{i}^{\top}\Bigr)\Bigr|. (71)

Let ZS⁡(w)∈ℝd×KZ_{S(w)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} and Z~S⁡(w)∈ℝE×K\tilde{Z}_{S(w)}\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times K} denote the feature matrices of the selected subset, let DS⁡(w)​(w):=diag​(wi)i∈S⁡(w)D_{S(w)}(w):=\text{diag}(w_{i})_{i\in S(w)}, and let GS⁡(w):=ZS⁡(w)⊤​ZS⁡(w)G_{S(w)}:=Z_{S(w)}^{\top}Z_{S(w)} and G~S⁡(w):=Z~S⁡(w)⊤​Z~S⁡(w)\tilde{G}_{S(w)}:=\tilde{Z}_{S(w)}^{\top}\tilde{Z}_{S(w)} denote the corresponding unweighted Gram matrices. By Sylvester’s determinant identity, the above difference can be rewritten as the discrepancy between logdet(IK+DS⁡(w)(w)12GS⁡(w)DS⁡(w)(w)12)\log\det\bigl(I_{K}+D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}G_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr) and logdet(IK+DS⁡(w)(w)12G~S⁡(w)DS⁡(w)(w)12)\log\det\bigl(I_{K}+D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{G}_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr).

Assume that projection and whitening preserve the local weighted Gram geometry of the selected subset in the sense that

‖DS⁡(w)​(w)12​G~S⁡(w)​DS⁡(w)​(w)12−DS⁡(w)​(w)12​GS⁡(w)​DS⁡(w)​(w)12‖2≤εpw​(S⁡(w),w).\bigl\|D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{G}_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}-D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}G_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\text{pw}}(S(w),w). (72)

Then, by the matrix mean value theorem, there exists a positive semidefinite matrix 𝐇S⁡(w),w\mathbf{H}_{S(w),w} on the segment between the two weighted Gram matrices such that

|Fspr​(w)−Fpw​(w)|\displaystyle\bigl|F_{\text{spr}}(w)-F_{\text{pw}}(w)\bigr| (73)
≤β​‖(IK+𝐇S⁡(w),w)−1‖2\displaystyle\leq\beta\|(I_{K}+\mathbf{H}_{S(w),w})^{-1}\|_{2}
⋅‖DS⁡(w)​(w)12​G~S⁡(w)​DS⁡(w)​(w)12−DS⁡(w)​(w)12​GS⁡(w)​DS⁡(w)​(w)12‖∗\displaystyle\cdot\bigl\|D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{G}_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}-D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}G_{S(w)}D_{S(w)}(w)^{\frac{1}{2}}\bigr\|_{*}

Since 𝐇S⁡(w),w⪰0\mathbf{H}_{S(w),w}\succeq 0, we have ‖(IK+𝐇S⁡(w),w)−1‖2≤1\|(I_{K}+\mathbf{H}_{S(w),w})^{-1}\|_{2}\leq 1. Using ‖M‖∗≤K​‖M‖2\|M\|_{*}\leq K\|M\|_{2} for any K×KK\times K matrix MM, we obtain

|Fspr​(w)−Fpw​(w)|≤β​K​εpw​(S⁡(w),w).\bigl|F_{\text{spr}}(w)-F_{\text{pw}}(w)\bigr|\leq\beta K\varepsilon_{\text{pw}}(S(w),w). (74)

The final term corresponds to the discrepancy introduced by replacing the full log-determinant of the projected covariance matrix with its diagonal surrogate. By the definition of Δdiag​(w)\Delta_{\text{diag}}(w) and the analysis in Appendix C.3, this term satisfies

|Fpw​(w)−F~​(w)|=β​Δdiag​(w),\bigl|F_{\text{pw}}(w)-\tilde{F}(w)\bigr|=\beta\,\Delta_{\text{diag}}(w), (75)

where Δdiag​(w)≥0\Delta_{\text{diag}}(w)\geq 0 denotes the diagonal approximation gap. Combining Eqs. (70), (74), and (75) with Eq. (69) yields

|Fdisc​(S⁡(w))−F~​(w)|≤L​‖w−𝟏S⁡(w)‖1+ν2​‖w‖22⏟Relaxation Gap+β​K​εpw​(S⁡(w),w)⏟Projection Gap+β​Δdiag​(w)⏟Diagonal Approx. Gap.\bigl|F_{\text{disc}}(S(w))-\tilde{F}(w)\bigr|\leq\underbrace{L\|w-\mathbf{1}_{S(w)}\|_{1}+\frac{\nu}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{Relaxation Gap}}+\underbrace{\beta\,K\,\varepsilon_{\text{pw}}(S(w),w)}_{\text{Projection Gap}}+\underbrace{\beta\,\Delta_{\text{diag}}(w)}_{\text{Diagonal Approx. Gap}}. (76)

Accordingly, under the local weighted-Gram preservation assumption, the gap between Eq. (4) and Eq. (7) is governed by the relaxation gap, projection-and-whitening distortion, and diagonal log-determinant approximation gap. When these terms are controlled, the surrogate in Eq. (7) remains close to the original utility–diversity objective in Eq. (4).

C.7.2 Analysis of Near-Optimality Under the Original Discrete Objective

The discrepancy bound above can be pushed one step further. Beyond objective-value closeness between Eq. (7) and Eq. (4), it shows that maximizing the surrogate yields a subset whose value under the original discrete objective is near-optimal up to an explicit error term.

To connect the pointwise discrepancy bound to optimizer behavior, define the feasible sparse set 𝒲K:={w⪰0:‖w‖0=K}\mathcal{W}_{K}:=\{w\succeq 0:\|w\|_{0}=K\} and, for any w∈𝒲Kw\in\mathcal{W}_{K}, the aggregated discrepancy term

Γ⁡(w):=L​‖w−𝟏S⁡(w)‖1+ν2​‖w‖22+β​K​εpw​(S⁡(w),w)+β​Δdiag​(w).\Gamma(w):=L\|w-\mathbf{1}_{S(w)}\|_{1}+\frac{\nu}{2}\|w\|_{2}^{2}+\beta K\varepsilon_{\text{pw}}(S(w),w)+\beta\Delta_{\text{diag}}(w). (77)

Here, Γ⁡(w)\Gamma(w) aggregates the relaxation, regularization, projection-whitening, and diagonal-approximation errors between the surrogate and original discrete objectives. Then Eq. (76) becomes

|Fdisc​(S⁡(w))−F~​(w)|≤Γ⁡(w),∀w∈𝒲K.\bigl|F_{\text{disc}}(S(w))-\tilde{F}(w)\bigr|\leq\Gamma(w),\qquad\forall\,w\in\mathcal{W}_{K}. (78)

Now let w^∈arg⁡maxw∈𝒲K​F~​(w)\hat{w}\in\arg\max_{w\in\mathcal{W}_{K}}\tilde{F}(w) and S^:=S⁡(w^)\hat{S}:=S(\hat{w}), and let S∗∈arg⁡maxS⊆𝒴,|S|=K​Fdisc​(S)S^{*}\in\arg\max_{S\subseteq\mathcal{Y},\ |S|=K}F_{\text{disc}}(S) denote an optimal subset of the original discrete objective. Define w∗:=𝟏S∗∈𝒲Kw^{*}:=\mathbf{1}_{S^{*}}\in\mathcal{W}_{K}. Applying Eq. (78) to w^\hat{w} gives Fdisc​(S^)≥F~​(w^)−Γ⁡(w^)F_{\text{disc}}(\hat{S})\geq\tilde{F}(\hat{w})-\Gamma(\hat{w}). Since w^\hat{w} maximizes F~\tilde{F} over 𝒲K\mathcal{W}_{K}, we have F~​(w^)≥F~​(w∗)\tilde{F}(\hat{w})\geq\tilde{F}(w^{*}). Applying Eq. (78) to w∗w^{*} gives F~​(w∗)≥Fdisc​(S∗)−Γ⁡(w∗)\tilde{F}(w^{*})\geq F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*})-\Gamma(w^{*}). Combining these inequalities yields Fdisc​(S^)≥Fdisc​(S∗)−Γ⁡(w^)−Γ⁡(w∗)F_{\text{disc}}(\hat{S})\geq F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*})-\Gamma(\hat{w})-\Gamma(w^{*}). When both endpoint discrepancies satisfy Γ⁡(w^)≤Γ¯\Gamma(\hat{w})\leq\bar{\Gamma} and Γ⁡(w∗)≤Γ¯\Gamma(w^{*})\leq\bar{\Gamma}, we obtain Fdisc​(S^)≥Fdisc​(S∗)−2​Γ¯F_{\text{disc}}(\hat{S})\geq F_{\text{disc}}(S^{*})-2\bar{\Gamma}.

Therefore, Eq. (78) further implies subset-level consistency. When the discrepancy terms are controlled at both the surrogate maximizer w^\hat{w} and the discrete optimum indicator w∗w^{*}, the subset induced by the surrogate maximizer remains within an explicit gap of 2​Γ¯2\bar{\Gamma} from the optimum of the original discrete objective. This extends the previous discrepancy analysis from objective-value approximation to optimizer-level consistency, indicating that Eq. (7) remains connected to the original utility–diversity objective beyond pointwise objective values. Appendix D.6 further examines this subset-level consistency empirically by comparing the subsets selected by NADS, Fast Greedy, and Lazy-Fast Greedy under the original discrete objective FdiscF_{\text{disc}}.

Appendix D Validation Experiments for Theoretical Analysis

D.1 Trajectory Mismatch and Ordering Fidelity

Appendix B.3 gives a local perturbation view of navigator-side forgetting-risk ordering. The navigator follows the unconstrained adaptation trajectory, whereas the final model is trained with KD regularization on the selected constraint set. Thus, the two trajectories need not coincide. This does not conflict with the role of the navigator in NADS, since the navigator is used to rank candidate samples by forgetting-aware utility rather than to reproduce the exact final training trajectory. We therefore examine whether the navigator preserves the ordering of forgetting-sensitive candidates when the final constrained trajectory deviates from the unconstrained one.

We conduct this analysis on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B. We fix the navigator and the synthetic candidate pool, and vary the KD strength over λ∈{0.1,1,5,10,50}\lambda\in\{0.1,1,5,10,50\} when training the final model. For each λ\lambda, we quantify trajectory mismatch by measuring the symmetric divergence between the predictive behaviors of the navigator and the final model on a fixed diagnostic subset 𝒞diag\mathcal{C}_{\text{diag}} as

Mismatch=1|𝒞diag|∑xi∈𝒞diag1|xi|∑t=1|xi|DJS(Pnav(⋅∣xi,<t)∥Pfinal(⋅∣xi,<t)).\text{Mismatch}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{\text{diag}}|}\sum_{x_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\text{diag}}}\frac{1}{|x_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|x_{i}|}D_{\text{JS}}\left(P_{\text{nav}}(\cdot\mid x_{i,<t})\|P_{\text{final}}(\cdot\mid x_{i,<t})\right). (79)

This metric captures how far the constrained final model moves away from the navigator’s unconstrained adaptation behavior at the prediction level. We then evaluate whether this deviation changes the utility-induced ordering of candidate samples by comparing the navigator-based scores with final-trajectory reference scores using Spearman correlation and Overlap@KK, where KK follows the same constraint-set budget as in the main experiments.

As shown in Fig. 7, larger λ\lambda increases the predictive-behavior mismatch between the navigator and the final model. This is consistent with the KD objective, where stronger distillation pulls the final model closer to the pretrained distribution on selected constraints. Importantly, ordering fidelity remains high near the default NADS setting. At λ=5\lambda=5, Spearman is 0.940.94 and Overlap@KK is 0.780.78, showing that the navigator still provides a reliable ranking signal for forgetting-aware constraint selection. Under the stress setting λ=50\lambda=50, the mismatch grows substantially and both ordering metrics decline, indicating that overly strong preservation constraints can disrupt ranking agreement. These results support the intended use of the navigator as a ranking proxy: exact trajectory matching is unnecessary as long as the ordering of forgetting-sensitive candidates is preserved within the practical mismatch range induced by the KD objective.

D.2 Utility Ranking Stability Across Navigator Checkpoints

The ordering analysis in Appendix B.3 provides a local and conditional view of when navigator-induced utility rankings can be preserved under small changes of the navigator state. We further verify this local view experimentally by examining whether the NADS utility ranking remains stable across nearby navigator checkpoints. To this end, we recompute the utility scores on the same candidate pool using navigator checkpoints from different stages of the unconstrained adaptation trajectory.

We use the three navigator checkpoints Mnav−1M_{\text{nav}}-1, Mnav−2M_{\text{nav}}-2, and Mnav−3M_{\text{nav}}-3 considered in Fig. 3(c). For each checkpoint s∈{1,2,3}s\in\{1,2,3\}, we compute the NADS utility score ui(s)u_{i}^{(s)} for every candidate sample xix_{i}, and obtain the corresponding score-induced ranking. We then measure the ranking agreement between two checkpoints using Spearman correlation and top-KK overlap, defined as

Overlap​(a,b)=|TopK​(u(a))∩TopK​(u(b))|K.\text{Overlap}(a,b)=\frac{\left|\text{TopK}\!\left(u^{(a)}\right)\cap\text{TopK}\!\left(u^{(b)}\right)\right|}{K}.

Spearman correlation evaluates global ranking consistency over the candidate pool, while top-KK overlap focuses on whether the high-utility candidates used for constraint construction remain stable.

As shown in Table 6, adjacent navigator checkpoints show stronger ranking agreement than the distant pair, suggesting that the utility ranking is locally consistent along the unconstrained adaptation trajectory but changes across substantially different navigator stages. This agrees with the checkpoint sensitivity in Fig. 3(c): an early navigator may stay too close to the pretrained model and provide a weak drift signal, whereas an overly late navigator may reflect excessive task-induced drift. Overall, this diagnostic supports the local ordering view in Appendix B.3 and explains the navigator-stage sensitivity in Fig. 3(c) at the ranking level.

D.3 Utility Ranking and Constraint Effectiveness

Appendix B.4 establishes a local connection between the KL-based utility and the KD discrepancy in final training. Motivated by the utility–degradation correlation in Fig. 2, we examine whether the utility ranking translates into effective preservation constraints. We split the candidate pool into high-, middle-, and low-utility ranges by the NADS score. From each range, we select a diverse constraint set with the same budget KK, then train the final model with the same DnewD_{\text{new}}, KD objective, distillation weight, and training recipe. Thus, variants differ only in the utility range used for DconstraintD_{\text{constraint}}.

Specifically, the high-, middle-, and low-utility ranges contain the top, middle, and bottom 20%20\% of candidates ranked by NADS utility, respectively. Within each range, we apply the same diversity-aware subset construction procedure to select KK constraint samples. We also include NADS, which performs utility–diversity selection over the full candidate pool, as the reference.

As shown in Table 7, high-utility constraint sets yield stronger general-capability retention than middle- and low-utility sets, while target performance remains stable. This shows that the utility score not only correlates with navigator-side degradation but also provides a useful ranking signal for preservation-constraint construction. Full NADS performs best, suggesting that hard truncation to one utility range is less effective than joint utility–diversity selection over the full candidate pool. These results further support navigator utility as a preservation-oriented signal for constraint construction.

D.4 Consistency of the Scalable Selection Surrogate

Appendix C.3 analyzes the approximation gap introduced by replacing the full log-determinant diversity term with its diagonal surrogate. We further examine this approximation experimentally in the selection stage. The diversity term in NADS is based on a log-determinant objective, but repeatedly evaluating the full log-det term over high-dimensional features is computationally expensive. To make selection scalable, we use projected and whitened features and replace the full log-det diversity term with a diagonal surrogate. This surrogate is efficient, but it should preserve the behavior of the full diversity objective used for subset selection. We therefore examine the consistency between the diagonal surrogate and the full log-det diversity term.

Let 𝒛~i∈ℝE\tilde{\bm{z}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{E} be the projected feature of sample xix_{i}. For a candidate subset SS, define 𝑨⁡(S)=∑i∈S𝒛~i​𝒛~i⊤\bm{A}(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\tilde{\bm{z}}_{i}\tilde{\bm{z}}_{i}^{\top}. The full and diagonal log-det diversity terms are Dfull(S)=logdet(𝑰+𝑨(S))D_{\text{full}}(S)=\log\det\left(\bm{I}+\bm{A}(S)\right) and Ddiag​(S)=∑e=1Elog⁡(1+Ae​e​(S))D_{\text{diag}}(S)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\log\left(1+A_{ee}(S)\right), respectively. Since the diagonal surrogate ignores the off-diagonal structure of 𝑨⁡(S)\bm{A}(S), we measure the relative strength of the ignored component. Let 𝑹⁡(S)=𝑨⁡(S)−diag​(𝑨⁡(S))\bm{R}(S)=\bm{A}(S)-\text{diag}(\bm{A}(S)). We report the off-diagonal ratio

OffDiagRatio​(S)=‖𝑹⁡(S)‖F‖𝑨⁡(S)‖F+ϵ,\text{OffDiagRatio}(S)=\frac{\|\bm{R}(S)\|_{F}}{\|\bm{A}(S)\|_{F}+\epsilon}, (80)

and the relative diagonal approximation gap

RelGapdiag​(S)=|Dfull​(S)−Ddiag​(S)||Dfull​(S)|+ϵ.\text{RelGap}_{\text{diag}}(S)=\frac{\left|D_{\text{full}}(S)-D_{\text{diag}}(S)\right|}{\left|D_{\text{full}}(S)\right|+\epsilon}. (81)

Both metrics are lower when the diagonal surrogate is a tighter approximation. We further evaluate whether the surrogate preserves the ranking behavior of the full diversity objective by computing the Spearman correlation between DfullD_{\text{full}} and DdiagD_{\text{diag}} over candidate subsets of the same size.

As shown in Fig. 8, projection-only features exhibit the largest off-diagonal ratio and relative diagonal gap, indicating that the diagonal surrogate is less consistent with the full log-det diversity term when feature correlations are not reduced. After whitening, both metrics decrease substantially. For the default setting E=256E=256, the off-diagonal ratio decreases from 0.3920.392 to 0.2290.229, and the relative diagonal gap decreases from 0.1420.142 to 0.0820.082. This supports the role of whitening in reducing the off-diagonal structure ignored by the diagonal approximation.

The rank-consistency results further show that the diagonal surrogate preserves the subset-ranking behavior of the full diversity term. Projection-only features achieve a Spearman correlation of 0.9020.902, while whitening improves the correlation across all projected dimensions. Although E=128E=128 yields the smallest approximation gap, its rank consistency is lower than that of E=256E=256, suggesting stronger projection-induced information loss. The default setting E=256E=256 achieves the highest rank correlation of 0.9640.964 while keeping the approximation gap low. Increasing the dimension to E=512E=512 slightly increases the off-diagonal ratio and approximation gap, with no further gain in rank consistency. These results provide experimental support for the diagonal approximation analysis in Appendix C.3. They show that whitening reduces the off-diagonal structure ignored by the diagonal surrogate, and that the default setting E=256E=256 largely preserves the ranking behavior of the full log-determinant diversity term while keeping the approximation gap low.

D.5 Validation of the Diagonal Log-Determinant Bound

Appendix C.3 derives a split-spectrum upper bound for the diagonal log-determinant approximation gap. We evaluate both sides of this bound on the final constraint set selected by NADS under the default setting. Let Δdiag=Ddiag−Dfull\Delta_{\text{diag}}=D_{\text{diag}}-D_{\text{full}} denote the observed Hadamard gap. Following Appendix C.3, the corresponding upper bound is

Bsplit=12​∑λj≥0λj2⏟B++12​∑λj<0λj2(1+λj)2⏟B−,B_{\text{split}}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}\geq 0}\lambda_{j}^{2}}_{B_{+}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\lambda_{j}<0}\frac{\lambda_{j}^{2}}{(1+\lambda_{j})^{2}}}_{B_{-}}, (82)

where λj\lambda_{j} are the eigenvalues of the normalized off-diagonal coupling matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C}. Fig. 9 evaluates the C.3 bound in the actual selection setting. The observed gap Δdiag=64.45\Delta_{\text{diag}}=64.45 lies below the split-spectrum certificate Bsplit=1206.65B_{\text{split}}=1206.65, with Δdiag/Bsplit=0.053\Delta_{\text{diag}}/B_{\text{split}}=0.053. This shows that the diagonal approximation gap on the final selected constraint set satisfies the theoretical upper bound. Meanwhile, the relative gap between the diagonal surrogate and the full log-determinant term is only 2.40%2.40\%, indicating that the scalable surrogate remains close to the full diversity term on the selected support.

The decomposition into B+B_{+} and B−B_{-} also follows the structure of Appendix C.3. The bound separates standard positive-spectrum contributions from the negative-spectrum branch that controls the worst-case log-determinant behavior. Thus, the certificate supports the split-spectrum bound on the actual selected support while keeping the interpretation appropriately conservative.

D.6 Consistency Analysis of the Optimization Objective

To further support the scalable selection strategy introduced in Sec. 3.4, we examine whether the subsets selected by NADS remain consistent with the original utility–diversity objective. We compare NADS with two greedy baselines, Fast Greedy [31] and Lazy-Fast Greedy [32], by evaluating all selected subsets under the original discrete objective FdiscF_{\text{disc}} in Eq. (4).

We sample a candidate pool of size 30,00030{,}000 from the synthetic dataset and select 10001000 samples in each trial. We repeat this procedure over 100100 independent random trials. For each comparison, let SNADS(t)S_{\text{NADS}}^{(t)} and SGreedy(t)S_{\text{Greedy}}^{(t)} denote the subsets returned by NADS and the corresponding greedy baseline in the tt-th trial, respectively. Here, SGreedy(t)S_{\text{Greedy}}^{(t)} refers to the subset selected by either Fast Greedy or Lazy-Fast Greedy in the corresponding comparison. We evaluate both subsets using the original discrete objective Fdisc​(⋅)F_{\text{disc}}(\cdot) in Eq. (4) and plot the paired values xt=Fdisc​(SGreedy(t))x_{t}=F_{\text{disc}}(S_{\text{Greedy}}^{(t)}) and yt=Fdisc​(SNADS(t))y_{t}=F_{\text{disc}}(S_{\text{NADS}}^{(t)}), so that each point (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}) in Fig. 10 corresponds to one random trial under one greedy comparison. The dashed line denotes y=xy=x. Points above this line indicate that NADS achieves a higher objective value than the corresponding greedy baseline under the original discrete objective.

To quantify the signed deviation from the greedy solution, we define

Δrel(t)=Fdisc​(SNADS(t))−Fdisc​(SGreedy(t))Fdisc​(SGreedy(t)).\Delta_{\text{rel}}^{(t)}=\frac{F_{\text{disc}}(S_{\text{NADS}}^{(t)})-F_{\text{disc}}(S_{\text{Greedy}}^{(t)})}{F_{\text{disc}}(S_{\text{Greedy}}^{(t)})}. (83)

Points on the diagonal satisfy xt=ytx_{t}=y_{t} and therefore correspond to zero objective gap. As shown in Fig. 10, most points remain close to the diagonal across random trials and greedy comparisons. This indicates that the subsets selected by the scalable NADS procedure achieve objective values close to those of the greedy baselines when evaluated under the original discrete objective. The result suggests that the proposed approximation does not substantially deviate from the behavior of the original utility–diversity objective while enabling scalable selection.

Appendix E Experimental Details

In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of the experimental setup for reproducibility. Section E.1 introduces the implementation and configurations of the baselines. Sections E.2 and E.3 describe the benchmarks and evaluation details used in our experiments. Section E.4 further presents the implementation details, including hyperparameter settings and training configurations. Section E.5 describes the navigator training and validation setting for checkpoint selection.

E.1 Baseline Details

We compare NADS against SOTA methods spanning PEFT, replay-based constraint selection methods, and target-data selection methods.

  • •

    Standard Fine-Tuning (Standard FT): This baseline updates all model parameters using the standard cross-entropy loss. It typically suffers from severe catastrophic forgetting and thus serves as a lower-bound reference for general capability preservation.

  • •

    LoRA [90]: This baseline injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into the Transformer layers while freezing the backbone parameters. Restricting the number of trainable parameters can itself effectively mitigate forgetting [18].

  • •

    InsCL [91]: InsCL is a replay-based method that selects replay data using instruction similarity measured by Wasserstein distance, and uses the instruction information metric InsInfo to characterize instruction complexity and diversity. By jointly training on target-task data and selected replay samples, InsCL mitigates catastrophic forgetting while preserving target-task adaptation.

  • •

    LER [92]: LER is a replay-based method that uses Leitner queuing, a human-inspired spaced repetition strategy, to select which historical samples should be replayed at each stage of learning. By prioritizing informative samples and adaptively scheduling their replay according to learning status, LER mitigates catastrophic forgetting while preserving adaptation to new data.

  • •

    Mix-cd [52]: Mix-cd is a replay-based method that selects and replays collateral damage samples, which are correctly predicted by the previous model but forgotten after incremental fine-tuning. By incorporating these selected samples into new-task training, Mix-cd mitigates catastrophic forgetting while improving the retention of previously acquired capabilities.

  • •

    LESS [59]: LESS is a selection method. It estimates the influence of training samples in an optimizer-aware manner and selects data by low-rank gradient similarity search with respect to a small set of target examples. By training on the selected subset, LESS improves adaptation to the target capability while substantially reducing the amount of training data required.

  • •

    FisherSFT [93]: FisherSFT is a selection-based method that selects training examples by maximizing information gain under the SFT objective, quantified via the Fisher information matrix. To make this objective practical for large language models, it adopts a last-layer linearization approximation, which enables efficient subset selection. Fine-tuning on the resulting subset improves adaptation efficiency while reducing the amount of training data required.

  • •

    SPICE [94]: SPICE is a selection-based method using a conflict-aware selector to balance sample informativeness and gradient alignment, while improving efficiency with early stopping and proxy models. Fine-tuning on the selected subset improves target performance at lower selection cost.

E.2 Training Data Details

In our experiments, we consider two target training datasets: code generation and mathematical reasoning. For code generation, we use Magicoder [80], a decontaminated code dataset. For mathematical reasoning, we use MetaMathQA [81], a large-scale mathematical question-answering dataset constructed by augmenting questions from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH. In addition, we adopt Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered [82] as a large-scale synthetic dataset, generated with the Magpie pipeline using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. Detailed dataset statistics are summarized in Table 8.

E.3 Evaluation Details

We evaluate model performance from two perspectives: general capability retention and target-task performance. Following recent studies [9, 10, 11, 83, 84], we decouple them to assess task adaptation and preservation of pre-existing abilities, with benchmark roles adjusted across fine-tuning scenarios. For models fine-tuned on Magicoder [80], HumanEval [85] is the target-task benchmark for code generation, while HellaSwag [87], OpenBookQA [89], MMLU [86], and GSM8K [88] evaluate general capability retention. For models fine-tuned on MetaMathQA [81], GSM8K is the target-task benchmark for mathematical reasoning, while HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, MMLU, and HumanEval evaluate general capability retention. Here, HumanEval serves as an out-of-domain benchmark for retained code generation ability after math fine-tuning. Table 9 summarizes the settings. All benchmarks are evaluated with lm-evaluation-harness [102] using standard prompting setups. General Capability Avg. is the arithmetic mean over the four general-capability benchmarks, and Overall Avg. is the arithmetic mean of General Capability Avg. and target-task performance.

  • •

    HellaSwag: HellaSwag [87] is a challenge dataset for commonsense natural language inference. Given an event description or partial context, the model is required to choose the most plausible continuation from several candidate endings. The dataset is constructed via Adversarial Filtering, where a series of discriminators iteratively select adversarial machine-generated negative options, making the benchmark easy for humans but substantially more difficult for SOTA models. Models are typically evaluated using the Accuracy metrics.

  • •

    OpenBookQA: Open Book Question Answering [89] is a question-answering dataset inspired by open-book exams for evaluating a model’s understanding of a subject. It consists of elementary-school-level multiple-choice science questions and assesses both the understanding of a core set of science facts and the ability to apply this knowledge to new situations. Models are typically evaluated using the Accuracy metric.

  • •

    MMLU: Massive Multitask Language Understanding [86] is a benchmark for evaluating the broad knowledge and reasoning abilities of models across multiple domains. It covers 57 subjects spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional knowledge. The dataset consists of multiple-choice questions, each with four or five answer options. For each subject, the model is required to select the correct answer based on its knowledge and reasoning. Models are typically evaluated using the Accuracy metric.

  • •

    GSM8K: Grade School Math 8K [88] is a benchmark dataset for evaluating the mathematical reasoning ability of models. It consists of grade-school-level math word problems, each accompanied by a step-by-step solution. Given a natural language problem, the model is required to generate a solution containing the correct numerical answer. The questions range from simple arithmetic to more complex multi-step reasoning. Models are typically evaluated using the EM metric.

  • •

    HumanEval: HumanEval [85] is a benchmark dataset proposed to evaluate the functional correctness of code generation models. It consists of 164 Python programming problems and is commonly evaluated using the PASS@1 metric. Given a problem description and a function signature, the model is required to generate Python code that implements the specified function. A generated solution is considered correct if it passes all provided unit tests.

We report three evaluation metrics in our experiments, which are defined as follows.

  • •

    Accuracy (ACC): Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions among all evaluation examples. Compared with Exact Match, it is less strict, as it allows multiple acceptable answers for a single example. Formally, it is defined as

    ACC=1N​∑i=1N𝕀⁡(y^i∈Yi),\text{ACC}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{i}\in Y_{i}), (84)

    where NN denotes the total number of evaluation examples, y^i\hat{y}_{i} is the model prediction for the ii-th example, and YiY_{i} denotes the set of acceptable ground-truth answers for that example.

  • •

    Exact Match (EM): Exact Match measures whether the predicted answer exactly matches the reference answer after normalization. Compared with Accuracy, it is stricter because it requires an exact match between the predicted output and the gold answer string. Formally, it is defined as

    EM=1N​∑i=1N𝕀⁡(y^i=yi),\text{EM}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_{i}=y_{i}), (85)

    where y^i\hat{y}_{i} and yiy_{i} denote the predicted and reference answers for the ii-th example, respectively.

  • •

    PASS@k: PASS@k is a standard metric for code generation. For each problem, the model generates kk candidate solutions, and the metric estimates the probability that at least one solution passes all associated unit tests. Formally, it is defined as

    PASS​@​k={1−(n−ck)(nk),if ​n−c≥k,1,if ​n−c<k,\text{PASS}@k=\begin{cases}1-\dfrac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},&\text{if }n-c\geq k,\\ 1,&\text{if }n-c<k,\end{cases} (86)

    where nn denotes the total number of generated solutions, cc denotes the number of correct solutions among them, and kk is the number of sampled solutions used for evaluation.

E.4 Implementation Details

All methods are implemented under a unified fine-tuning setup and optimized with AdamW using a cosine learning-rate scheduler. For Magicoder, we use a global batch size of 64, maximum sequence length 4096, and 3 training epochs; for MetaMathQA, we use a global batch size of 128, maximum sequence length 1024, and 2 epochs. The warmup ratio is 0.03 in both settings. For each target dataset, we hold out 1,0001{,}000 examples for validation and use the remaining target-training split for all methods. NADS uses the entire target-training split for target-task learning and selects 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}} from the synthetic candidate pool 𝒞\mathcal{C}, with size fixed at 5%5\% of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Replay-based constraint selection methods, including Random selection, InsCL [91], LER [92], and Mix-cd [52], use the same target-training split and replay size. Target-data selection methods, including LESS [59], FisherSFT [93], and SPICE [94], select 10%10\% of the target-training split without using 𝒟constraint\mathcal{D}_{\text{constraint}}. We use official repositories for all baselines except LER and Mix-cd, whose code is unavailable. For NADS, we set the confidence gate γ=0.7\gamma=0.7, regularization ν=3×10−3\nu=3\times 10^{-3}, diversity β=1.0\beta=1.0, distillation λ=5\lambda=5, IHT iterations T=50T=50, and projection dimension E=256E=256. We tune the learning rate for all methods in [1×10−5, 5×10−4][1\times 10^{-5},\,5\times 10^{-4}] and report the best results. For NADS, the selected learning rates on Magicoder are 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}, and 7×10−57\times 10^{-5} for LLaMA3.2-3B, Gemma3-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B, respectively; on MetaMathQA, they are 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} and 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} for LLaMA3.2-3B and Gemma3-4B, respectively. All experiments are conducted on 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

E.5 Navigator Training and Validation Setting

For each target dataset, we construct the navigator by fine-tuning MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} on the target-task data without preservation regularization or constraint samples. The navigator follows the same target fine-tuning recipe as the final adaptation stage, including the optimizer, scheduler, batch size, maximum sequence length, warmup ratio, and training epochs. For navigator early stopping, we hold out 1,0001{,}000 examples from each of the two target datasets as the validation split and use the remaining examples for navigator training. During navigator training, we evaluate checkpoints every 500 training steps and select the checkpoint with the lowest target-task validation negative log-likelihood on the corresponding validation split as MnavM_{\text{nav}}.

Appendix F Experimental Results and Analysis

F.1 Results on MetaMathQA Benchmark

In this subsection, we present the experimental results on the MetaMathQA benchmark. We report results on LLaMA3.2-3B and Gemma3-4B. Qwen3.5-9B is not included in this setting because its mathematical performance is already strong before MetaMathQA fine-tuning, which leaves limited room for observing target-side adaptation and makes the trade-off analysis less informative.

Table 10 reports the results under each method’s native protocol. On LLaMA3.2-3B, NADS achieves 42.53% in general capability average and 53.86% in overall average, compared with 41.32% and 52.16% for the strongest baselines. On Gemma3-4B, NADS again obtains the best general capability average and overall average, reaching 45.75% and 56.14%, respectively. Although Standard FT achieves strong target performance, it suffers from a much larger degradation in general capability. In contrast, NADS maintains competitive target task performance while substantially improving general capability preservation, leading to the best overall trade off across both model architectures.

Table 11 further reports cross-paradigm reference results with methods that select samples from 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}. Since these methods optimize the target-task subset rather than construct synthetic constraint data, this comparison serves as an additional reference rather than a direct same-protocol comparison. Under this reference setting, NADS achieves the best overall average on both LLaMA3.2-3B and Gemma3-4B, while maintaining strong target-task performance. These reference results indicate that NADS achieves a favorable adaptation–preservation balance under the MetaMathQA setting, maintaining strong target-task performance while better preserving general capabilities.

F.2 Controlled comparison under the same KD objective

In the main experiments, selection-based baselines fine-tune on selected subsets, creating a training-scale mismatch with NADS. Since they use less new-task supervision, they naturally reduce update-induced drift and operate in a preservation-favorable setting. To test whether this mismatch explains the performance gap, we conduct a controlled comparison on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2 by equipping these baselines with the same final KD objective as NADS. For each baseline, we train a separate navigator on its selected subset and construct a navigator-guided constraint set from the same synthetic pool. We also include a random-constraint variant under the same KD objective. As shown in Table 12, random constraints do not reliably improve retention and can even reduce general capability, whereas navigator-guided constraints consistently improve general capability across selection-based baselines. This indicates that NADS gains are not merely from adding KD, but from selecting more effective retention constraints from the noisy and redundant synthetic pool. The consistent gains across LESS, FisherSFT, and SPICE further suggest that navigator-guided constraint construction is transferable rather than method-specific.

F.3 Checkpoint Selection across Models and Datasets

We evaluate Navigator checkpoint selection across five model–dataset combinations covering three models and two target datasets. All settings use the same validation-based early-stopping rule. We compare three checkpoints in each setting and report target-task, general-capability, and overall scores using a single seed. As shown in Table 13, Nav-2 selected by validation-based early stopping achieves the highest overall score in all five model–dataset combinations. This consistent result demonstrates the robustness of the checkpoint selection rule across different models and target datasets.

F.4 Sensitivity to Validation-Set Perturbations

We assess the sensitivity of Navigator checkpoint selection to validation-set quality and distribution on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2, comparing the original validation set with three variants: 20% label noise, 40% label noise, and template shift. Label noise replaces the corresponding proportion of target answers with other samples’ answers; template shift uses a template different from the test set to simulate validation–evaluation mismatch. Results are averaged over three seeds and include sample-utility Spearman correlation and Top-KK selection overlap relative to the original setting, alongside target-task, general-capability, and overall scores.

As shown in Table 14, utility rank correlations remain between 0.69 and 0.83, while Top-KK overlaps range from 0.58 to 0.72 across the three perturbed validation settings. Although the perturbations change utility rankings and selected samples, target-task, general-capability, and overall scores remain close to those obtained with the original validation set. These results support the robustness of Navigator-based data selection to the tested label noise and template shift.

F.5 Diversity Analysis of the Selected Data

The main text presents representative selected-data visualizations. Here, we provide additional t-SNE [99] visualizations and quantitative diversity diagnostics for more selection methods. As shown in Fig. 11, the DPP-based selector serves as a diversity-oriented reference and broadly covers the semantic space. The PPL-based selector ranks by perplexity and concentrates on dense semantic regions, indicating stronger redundancy. Mix-cd selects samples correctly predicted by the previous model but forgotten by the subsequent model, yielding broad coarse-cluster coverage but less consistent geometric spread. InsCL estimates task similarity via Wasserstein Distance and biases sampling toward high-quality data with InsInfo, giving broader coverage than PPL and Mix-cd but still showing local clustering. LER dynamically updates memory and selects samples by Leitner-based learnability, yet its samples remain less dispersed in the continuous representation space.

To complement the visualization, Fig. 12 reports four diversity diagnostics: average pairwise cosine distance, normalized cluster entropy, effective rank, and log-det diversity. They measure sample-level separation, coarse cluster coverage, active representation directions, and selected-set geometric volume, respectively. DPP achieves the highest values, as expected from its diversity-oriented objective. NADS remains close to DPP on high-dimensional geometric metrics, including pairwise distance, effective rank, and log-det diversity, while outperforming other non-DPP baselines. Its normalized cluster entropy is lower than DPP and Mix-cd but remains high, indicating broad cluster coverage without simply maximizing uniform coarse-cluster spread. These results show that NADS preserves strong selected-set diversity while incorporating preservation-oriented utility.

F.6 Computational Cost Analysis

In this section, we analyze the computational cost and performance–cost trade-off to show that the additional cost introduced by our method is acceptable and justified.

Selection Cost. Our setting aims to mitigate forgetting during fine-tuning while retaining gains on the new task, which requires estimating forgetting risk before the final training stage. NADS therefore uses a navigator to evaluate candidate samples. In the full-parameter setting, navigator training adds selection-stage cost. On Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B, it takes about 4 hours on 4 A100 GPUs, or 0.67 GPU-days. This one-time cost is incurred before final fine-tuning and remains practical at the considered scale. Appendix F.7 further examines a LoRA-based navigator as an efficient approximation, showing comparable performance with only a small drop. In the same setting, this variant uses 11.14 GB of GPU memory and takes about 3 hours on 4 A100 GPUs, or 0.5 GPU-days. Thus, although some baselines have lower selection overhead, the relevant comparison is the overall cost–performance trade-off, especially when severe forgetting must be controlled.

Performance–cost Trade-off. We further examine the performance–cost trade-off. Fig. 13 visualizes methods on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B by training cost, peak GPU memory, and overall score. All methods are run with a per-device micro-batch size of 2 and an effective global batch size of 64 through gradient accumulation. Target-data selection methods select 10% of the target-training data from 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}, whereas replay-based methods and NADS select 5% of the synthetic candidates from 𝒞\mathcal{C} as constraints, matching the main experimental setting. We therefore separate the two groups rather than treating them as a direct ranking. Within the constraint-selection group, NADS achieves the highest Overall score with moderate training cost and peak memory. This suggests that navigator-guided utility and diversity-aware subset construction provide a favorable effectiveness and efficiency balance for constructing preservation constraints.

F.7 Efficient Navigator Approximation with LoRA

The navigator model is designed to trace the unconstrained adaptation path under the target recipe and expose the predictive drift induced by new-task fine-tuning. In principle, its training recipe should match that of the final model, except that preservation constraints are removed, thereby providing a recipe-aligned probe of adaptation-induced forgetting. However, NADS uses the navigator only to induce sample-level drift scores over candidate constraint samples, rather than to reproduce the exact parameter trajectory of the final model. Thus, a LoRA-based navigator can serve as an efficient approximation if it preserves the relative ranking of candidate samples under the drift signal.

Specifically, we train a LoRA-based navigator by adapting MpretrainM_{\text{pretrain}} on 𝒟new\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}} without anti-forgetting regularization, using α=16\alpha=16 and rank r=32r=32. The resulting MnavLoRAM_{\text{nav}}^{\text{LoRA}} approximates unconstrained adaptation within a low-rank update subspace. To test whether it preserves the NADS selection signal, we compare it with a full-parameter navigator MnavFullM_{\text{nav}}^{\text{Full}} on Magicoder with LLaMA3.2-3B. Let siLoRAs_{i}^{\text{LoRA}} and siFulls_{i}^{\text{Full}} denote the forgetting-aware scores assigned to candidate xix_{i} by the two navigators. We measure their agreement using Spearman​({siLoRA}i=1N,{siFull}i=1N)\text{Spearman}\!\left(\{s_{i}^{\text{LoRA}}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{s_{i}^{\text{Full}}\}_{i=1}^{N}\right) and top-KK overlap:

Overlap@​K=|TopK​({siLoRA}i=1N)∩TopK​({siFull}i=1N)|K.\text{Overlap@}K=\frac{\left|\text{TopK}\left(\{s_{i}^{\text{LoRA}}\}_{i=1}^{N}\right)\cap\text{TopK}\left(\{s_{i}^{\text{Full}}\}_{i=1}^{N}\right)\right|}{K}. (87)

As shown in Table 15, the LoRA navigator achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.890.89 and an Overlap@KK of 0.820.82 with the full-parameter navigator, while reducing relative training time to 0.74×0.74\times and relative memory usage to 0.16×0.16\times. This indicates that LoRA preserves most of the sample-ranking signal needed for constraint selection while reducing navigator construction cost.

We further compare the final performance obtained with the two navigator instantiations under the same synthetic candidate pool, constraint selection procedure, and KD objective. As shown in Table 16, NADS with the LoRA navigator achieves performance close to that of the full-parameter navigator, with only a small decrease in general capability average, target performance, and overall score. Overall, these results show that the LoRA navigator provides an efficient approximation to the full-parameter navigator. Thus, LoRA is a practical option when navigator construction cost is a concern, while the full-parameter navigator remains the most recipe-matched instantiation.

F.8 Computational Cost across Model Sizes

We follow the evaluation convention adopted by closely related data-selection methods involving auxiliary training or scoring, including reference-model construction in DavIR [62] and RHO-1 [103], surrogate or warmup training in ToV [72] and LESS [59], and reference–proxy training in DoReMi [104]. Their main performance comparisons generally keep the final target-model training protocol fixed rather than reallocating auxiliary computational costs to longer baseline training. While comparisons under matched end-to-end computational budgets would provide a stricter assessment of computational fairness, we additionally report stage-wise and total costs to make this overhead explicit.

We compare the stage-wise and total computational costs of NADS on LLaMA3.2-3B, Gemma3-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B. All experiments use Magicoder and the same Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered candidate pool, with costs measured in GPU-hours. As shown in Table 17, NADS achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods on all three backbones, while subset optimization requires only 0.02 GPU-hours. The total cost increases from 44.82 to 113.43 GPU-hours as model size increases from 3B to 9B parameters. Using LoRA for navigator training reduces the 9B total cost to 97.28 GPU-hours while maintaining a comparable overall score of 68.13, versus 68.34 with full-parameter navigator training.

F.9 Effect of Constraint-Set Size

In this section, we study the effect of constraint-set size on NADS. Specifically, we vary the size of the selected constraint set and evaluate how it influences NADS in terms of general capability, target-task performance, and overall performance.

Table 18 reports results under different constraint-set sizes. When K=1%K=1\%, the subset is too small to provide sufficient preservation support. Increasing KK to 3%3\% and 5%5\% markedly improves performance, showing that larger constraint sets provide stronger preservation signals. At 10%10\%, performance continues to improve but with limited gain, suggesting saturation beyond a certain size. Thus, we use 5%5\% as the default budget to match the main replay setting while emphasizing efficiency. When KK further increases to 15%15\%, performance declines, indicating that overly large constraint sets may introduce redundant or less informative samples and weaken selective construction. Overall, increasing KK helps when the constraint set is small, but the benefit gradually saturates and can reverse when excessive samples are included.

F.10 Impact of Different Synthetic Datasets

In this section, we analyze the impact of synthetic datasets on NADS. NADS does not assume that the synthetic dataset used for constraint construction covers the model’s general capabilities. Instead, it treats the synthetic dataset as a candidate source for constructing the constraint set.

We compare Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered [82], Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-1M-v0.1 [82], Magpie-Llama-3.1-Pro-300K-Filtered [82], and WizardLM-evol-instruct-70k [105], covering both synthetic datasets of different scales and datasets of the same scale generated by different models. For fair comparison, we fix the constraint-set budget to 15,00015{,}000 samples for all datasets, corresponding to 5%5\% of Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered. We then construct the constraint set from each synthetic dataset and evaluate its impact on NADS.

Fig. 14 reports results on seven evaluation metrics. Compared with Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-300K-Filtered, Magpie-Qwen2.5-Pro-1M-v0.1 generally yields slightly better or more stable results, suggesting that a larger synthetic pool can better support constraint-set construction. Magpie-Llama-3.1-Pro-300K-Filtered shows noticeable differences on some metrics, indicating that the generator model also affects constraint quality at a fixed data scale. In contrast, WizardLM-evol-instruct-70k performs worse on several metrics, likely due to its smaller scale and limited candidate coverage. Overall, synthetic dataset choice affects NADS mainly through candidate-pool quality and coverage, while the overall variation remains moderate.

F.11 Results on Instruction Tuning

We further evaluate all methods by fine-tuning LLaMA3.2-3B on Alpaca-GPT4 [100] to assess broad instruction-tuning performance. Alpaca-GPT4 contains diverse instruction-following tasks, covering question answering, reasoning, writing, and formatting. For general capability, we report results on ARC-Challenge and ARC-Easy [106], PIQA [107], Winogrande [108], HellaSwag [87], OpenBookQA [89], TruthfulQA [109], MMLU [86], GSM8K [88], and HumanEval [85], and compute General Avg. as their arithmetic mean. Following recent instruction-tuning studies [110, 111, 112], we use IFEval [113] and report prompt-level strict accuracy (PS), instruction-level strict accuracy (IS), prompt-level loose accuracy (PL), instruction-level loose accuracy (IL), and their arithmetic mean as IFEval Avg. Overall performance is computed as the average of General Avg. and IFEval Avg. Following the main experimental setup, we fine-tune on Alpaca-GPT4 for 3 epochs with a global batch size of 128 and a maximum sequence length of 4096. For NADS, the learning rate selected on Alpaca-GPT4 is 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}.

Table 19 reports the Alpaca-GPT4 results. Standard FT improves IFEval Avg. from 29.78 to 36.26, while reducing performance on MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval relative to the pre-trained model. InsCL, LER, and Mix-cd further improve average instruction-following performance, with Mix-cd achieving the strongest baseline Overall score of 45.17. NADS achieves the highest General Avg., IFEval Avg., and Overall scores, reaching 52.45, 39.89, and 46.17, respectively. Among fine-tuned methods, NADS ranks first on all four IFEval metrics and eight of the ten general-capability benchmarks. These results demonstrate that NADS remains effective in broad instruction tuning, improving instruction following while preserving strong general capability.

Appendix G Comparison with Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation Methods

In this subsection, we compare NADS with representative catastrophic-forgetting mitigation methods, including STM [8], NANOADAM [101], FLOW [11], DavIR [62], and TALR [10]. Since this is a supplementary comparison beyond the main benchmark, we evaluate two datasets with two representative model backbones.

The full results on Magicoder and MetaMathQA are reported in Tables 21 and 21. Across both datasets and backbones, NADS achieves the best Overall Avg., indicating a more favorable balance between target-task adaptation and general capability preservation. On Magicoder, standard fine-tuning substantially improves the target task but clearly degrades general-capability benchmarks, reflecting the typical adaptation–preservation conflict. Existing mitigation methods reduce this degradation to varying degrees, but their preservation signals are parameter-centric, regularization-based, or not explicitly tied to forgetting induced by the current target-task update. Thus, they often improve one side of the trade-off while leaving noticeable loss on the other. In contrast, NADS constructs preservation constraints from navigator-induced predictive drift, aligning the replay signal more directly with capabilities affected by the current adaptation trajectory. This yields the best Overall Avg. on both LLaMA3.2-3B and Gemma3-4B, with consistently strong General Capability Avg. and competitive target-task performance.

On MetaMathQA, the same trend appears under a different target capability. Standard fine-tuning attains strong GSM8K performance but noticeably weakens general capabilities, while existing mitigation baselines only partially recover this balance. NADS achieves the best Overall Avg. and General Capability Avg. on both backbones, showing that the selected synthetic constraints preserve broad capabilities even when the target task shifts to mathematical reasoning. Meanwhile, NADS maintains highly competitive GSM8K performance, suggesting that the preservation constraints do not simply over-regularize the model toward the pretrained state. Overall, NADS improves the adaptation–preservation trade-off across both code and math fine-tuning settings, rather than merely increasing target performance or retention in isolation.

Appendix H Limitations

A main limitation of NADS lies in navigator construction. We obtain the navigator by following the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization, so its deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced drift. While simple and aligned with the adaptation process, this design makes the selection signal sensitive to the navigator checkpoint and training dynamics, and introduces an additional pre-selection cost before final fine-tuning. A navigator stopped too early may provide weak drift signals, whereas one trained too long may yield noisy or biased utility estimates. Although validation-based checkpoint selection and the cost analysis in Appendix F.6 support the practicality of this design, more adaptive and lower-cost navigator construction may further improve robustness across tasks and fine-tuning recipes.

Broader Impacts

NADS aims to make LLM fine-tuning more stable by selecting synthetic constraints that help preserve pretrained behavior during new-task adaptation. This may reduce capability degradation and lower the cost of safer model adaptation. However, preserved pretrained behavior and synthetic candidate pools may still contain biases, factual errors, or unsafe content. Deployments in sensitive domains should therefore include task-specific safety evaluation, data-quality review, and misuse-risk assessment. Our experiments use public datasets, benchmarks, and base models, and do not collect user data or involve human-subject studies.

Reproducibility

We will release code, configurations, prompt templates, and scripts for reproducing the main results. All datasets, benchmarks, synthetic candidate pools, and base models used in this work are publicly available. The repository will document preprocessing, split construction, navigator training, constraint selection, final fine-tuning, and evaluation commands.

Licenses and Assets

We use publicly available datasets, benchmarks, synthetic data sources, and base models under their respective licenses and terms of use. NADS does not introduce a new dataset. Released assets will include code, configurations, scripts, and prompt templates, and will not redistribute third-party datasets or model weights unless permitted by their licenses.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: The paper discusses the limitations of the work in Appendix H.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

    Experimental result reproducibility

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: We share our code and hyperparameters.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: We report results as mean ±\pm standard deviation over multiple runs for the main experiments. The standard deviation captures variability across different random seeds under the same experimental setting, and the evaluation protocol is described in the experimental section.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: We discuss computational resources used for all experiments in Appendix F.6.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: The research conducted in the paper conforms, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: We discuss both positive and negative impacts. NADS may improve fine-tuning stability and reduce capability degradation, but preserved pretrained behavior and synthetic candidate pools may still contain biases, factual errors, or unsafe content. We therefore recommend safety evaluation, data-quality review, and misuse-risk assessment for sensitive deployments.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: Our work proposes a training technique for mitigating catastrophic forgetting and does not release models or datasets that pose a high risk of misuse.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: We cite the public datasets, benchmarks, synthetic data sources, and base models used in this work, and state that they are used under their respective licenses and terms of use. Released assets will include only code, configurations, scripts, and prompt templates, and will not redistribute third-party datasets or model weights unless permitted by their licenses.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: We will release anonymized code, configurations, scripts, and prompt templates, with documentation describing preprocessing, split construction, navigator training, constraint selection, final fine-tuning, and evaluation commands.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.
